English: The native faith of the local Asyum people is reflexively that of the Jur cosmological scriptures and the many fables and texts about their various Gods. With their closed and secretive temples, crypts, and schools, it is difficult to know exactly what Gods are being worshiped by the J'ur. The Wapkam company has issued several regulations to restrict the worship of the J'ur faithful, as it is an offense to the Imperial Godhood. Yet they retain their old temple precincts, which have again surfaced as a topic of debate in the Congress of Estates. Apparently, a watchman attempted to force his entry into a J'ur temple on the grounds of various anti-cult laws. The J'ur faithful attempted to appeal to a company court, claiming they are not a cult, like the barbarous jungle faiths, or the blasphemous Vewugists, and in fact claimed they recognise the Pudwou as equivalent with one of their old gods. Not all J'ur honour the Pudwou, however, and the Congress is debating revised regulations on J'ur worship.

Our recent efforts to meddle in $FROMCOUNTRY$'s government have ended in disaster. Rather than accepting the changes we imposed upon them, they have raised their flag in rebellion, and broken the seal of our government!

Some time ago our government extended special privileges to the J'ur worshipers. Recently, a debate has emerged in the Congress of Estates about the status of the Asyum in general in society. As many years have passed, the Asyum J'ur have become, as it were, a second society to the Wapkam company, who have their allotted privileges within our state, and enjoy protection and security vis-a-vis the hoards of migrants that arrive daily at our shores. Certain factions in the Congress of Estates wish to extend representation of the Asyum temples in the Estates, to secure their loyalty to us, while others advocate for a strengthening of hereditary rights and privileges of the temples, and fashioning them into a subordinate guild hierarchy to ours. Still more members of the Estates reject outright these proposals, thinking that such innovations will be the end of Wapkami Society as we know it.
Wapkam Extends Protection to Pagan Temples!

Our spies and ambassadors in Wapkam have recently informed us that, recently, the Congress of Estates, the governors of the company, have passed a law, which has been approved by the President-Director, to elevate the J'ur temples to equal status to those maintained by the Imperial clergy in Wapkam! This is a horrendous insult to the Vopudwou, and tantamount to a denial of his divinity. The Congress alleges that the J'ur recognise, through their strange scriptures and many-faced Gods, the ultimate divinity of the Pudwou, and that their many strange Gods and Spirits are something akin to the divine-borrowing nobility and heroes of ancient Poumnia. This pathetic apology of their religious innovations has greatly angered the Imperial Clergy. While the Wapkam company has long been practically independent of us, the President-Director is still the titular viceroy of the Pudwou in the east, and this would be, at least, an embarrassment for us.
Imperial Clergy Declares Intention to Restore Orthodoxy

Our recent choice to extend religious privileges to the J'ur of Wapkam, it seems, has greatly displeased the Imperial government in Poumnia! They are accusing the Wapkam company of apostasy, and have, it seems, declared an intention to restore "correct doctrines and divine honours in the ancestral customs" by force of military arms! The President-Director has declared that he is now the official head to the Wapkami state, and the Estates have convened to attempt to organise a military resistance.
Poumnia is attempting to puppet, sphere and restore Wompowushan as the sole state religion in $RECIPIENT$.
Poumnia is attempting to puppet, sphere and restore Wompowushan as the sole state religion in $RECIPIENT$ for challening the divinity of the Poumnian Emperor
This country has only recently been subjugated, and is taking some time to get used to their new overlords.
The elites and the government in this country is largely in the hands of citizens of their foriegn overlord.

It appears the ancient might of the Pudwou has fallen. We are receiving reports that beyond the sea, rebel mobs have sacked Prousorum and deposed the very world soul in a traumatic and tumultuous rebellion. Politically, this changes very little for Wapkam. We have long been practically independent, but it certainly will challenge the reflexive faith of our people. What we have noticed, however, is a number of members of the old government have requested asylum in 'His Majesty's Extramarine Viceroyalty of Bafozh' as they continue to refer to us. The government must decide whether it is worth risking the ire of Poumnia to offer asylum for these old nobles.

The recent efforts by the state to restrict foreign immigration and smooth the path of the integration of strangers has led to a particularly interesting debate in the congress of estates in the great fortress of the directory in Aincha. An increasingly xenophobic tendency has made itself manifest - the 'protectionist' party has come to argue that any invitation of foreigners into the old Wapkami territories and guilds is foolish and hopeless endeavour - indeed, the city of Aincha and its environs were closed to even provincial Wapkami Company members in the early thirteenth century. But, not naively, they suggest that new lands should be opened up for exploitation, in the jungles and in the northern plains, to accommodate new migrants who seek to submit to the Wapkam company, and then only after this should the old guilds and settlements should be totally protected, exclusive to Rashuum usage.

Gold is a precious commodity, and it is incredibly rare. In fact, the total amount of gold dug up before the fourteenth century would scarcely fill up four large rooms. Nonetheless, it plays an important role in both the international currency market, and the commodity trade in many societies. Thus, it was of great interest to the treasury that it appears credible that a large gold vein has been discovered in $PROVINCE$ by prospectors. There is already a great hubbub in $CAPITAL$, with many declaring that they intend to pack their bags, travel the great distance to $PROVINCE$ and get rich. Doubtless, for many, this is not likely to happen, but the discovery bodes well for our state.

Some years ago, a great vein of gold was found in $PROVINCE$. $PROVINCE$ itself has become a byword for sudden and fantastical wealth, and many fortunes were both made and lost in prospecting and mining in $PROVINCE$. In recent years, however, it seems as if this fabled land of rivers of gold is becoming one of streams, and now droplets. The great gold mines of $PROVINCE$ are running dry. The eager prospectors are now packing up their bags, and mounting their swine to head to the next awaited great bonanza, and those who remain are left to try to scrounge up a little life in the undeveloped wastes.

In our currently politically vulnerable situation, it seems we have been given a premonition for further negative developments. One of our neighbours has recently elected to withdraw its ambassadorial staff, and shutter its consulates. This, it is felt, could mean only one thing: war. We must brace for this challenge!

Following our successful seizure of territories further into the Juruntine, the director-general has issued an order for the closure of the old settlements and territories. For most estates this means very little actual change in policy beyond a few more rejections of admission or transfer requests, though watchmen at sensitive points like exchanges, border posts, public granaries, mess halls, and factories are increasingly encouraged to check internal passports of labourers.

Our recent efforts to meddle in $FROMCOUNTRY$'s government have ended in disaster. Rather than accepting the changes we imposed upon them, they have raised their flag in rebellion, and broken the seal of our government!

The increasing influx of strangers to our land threatens to overthrow the delicate composition of Wapkami society... or so the argument goes. It is true that Wapkami society is a highly stratified one, with a highly corporate identity. An Poumnian settler society set amongst the sullen, silent faces of the Asyum natives, with their closed J'ur temples and connections with the dense jungle villages, we have had to become closed in, and secretive. We have had to be severe in our governance, too, to guard against internal threats to our order. For the Poumnian serf, transplanted from the grain paddies of the Poudwouvas, was wont to become wild, and contumacious when set in the vast sparsely settled coasts of the Juruntine. Thus, each settlement, from the lowest 'Dro', or planation, to the great 'Ouswun's (forts) of Aincha keeps its own guild (kuukriw) structure, with a delicate path for succession, progression, and the exclusion of strangers, all as part of the harmonious structure of the Wapkam company. However, a lack of care at the arrival of immigrants, nominally responsible to the 'Mroumou Sharotib Shadravamn' (Work Authority of Strangers), has led to their establishment of basically free and autonomous communities within Wapkami society. There are many cries for more distinct efforts to subjugate immigrants to a more strict integration into Wapkami society.

The stringent effort to restrict unfettered immigration of foreigners into Wapkam is, ultimately, a hindrance to our strength. Able bodies to work the fields, to die in wars, and to cut and haul lumber are more important than any social and administrative harmony to be gained by restricting immigration.

The extreme xenophobic wing of Wapkami society has long argued for the constitutional enshrinement of metical restrictions. The establishment of a strict 'metic' (in the Poumnian - 'Pkoau') class, unable to ever achieve any citizenship or member of any guild, or access certain supports or privileges, and whom are in fact typically shunted into servile or banausic work, would appease many nativist sentiments, and indeed would probably make life easier for even the lowest of the members of the company, but it is bound to create suboptimal conditions for labor allocation, and make our state less attractive to migrants.

The metical restrictions to our society are, overall, a burden, and it is time to repeal them. Those of merit and good birth should eventually be able to rise to higher ranks of our society, even if they were born abroad.

The dynamic Greatlord of the eastern domains, Gozomedes Midodazh, at the outset of his reign, marshaled massive forces to begin an invasion of the rebellious and fractured imperial provinces. His army laws disrupted the traditional dynamic of noble officers leading the sons of their serfs into battle, and created some of the first true massive armies. The scale of tactics prompted a pivot to wars of dynamic movement, and grand battles, as well as logistical and officerial innovations as the military staff gained increasing flexibility and responsibility. His vastly effective armies, as demonstrated most spectacularly in the battle of Adnozhkt, against the combined forces of the southern alliance, demanded the large adoption of Gozomedic tactics and scales of arms by most of the foremost early states of Ishafazh in the early parts of the fourteenth century.

In the years following increasingly dynamic and grand battles, there were redoubled efforts to innovate in the area of fortifications and syngerise them with the dramatic mobile warfare of the early fourteenth century. Innovations accumulated in carefully positioned fortresses as well as trenching, embankments, and sappers embedded in units to provide shelter for mobile artillery positions.

The advent of the railroad and especially its proliferation in the fractious territories in the Great Nâg encouraged the increased integration of civilian, military, and private railway organization in pursuit of military aims. Civilian and private entities worked closely with military authorities to ensure enough rolling stock for hasty mobilization, and timetables were communicated with the general staff
French: train conductors were either part of the soldiery or trained for mobilization patterns
German: and finally special transport corps were organized for embarking and disembarking on and from trains.

English: The "Two Legger" was a late fourteenth century landship pioneered in the substantial war between the Great Nâg and Poumnia. Consisting functionally of an combustion engine axel system that turns two massive front metal wheels supported by smaller auxiliary wheels at the back and a sheet metal skeleton, it features a back engine brig, a front gunnery hold to preserve a mounted artillery piece or machine gun, and a tall front cabin tower with a barred window for shooting and steering. The first and earliest two leggers saw service trundling across the shelled-out landscape of the frontlines in Dhuknâg. Its narrow tall structure with massive wheels made it easy to steer, and less liable to get stuck in muddy terrain, and even ford through small swamps, but it was liable to tip if hit directly by shells.

The early two legger deployments were usually clumsy or ill conceived. Two Leggers were hit by shells and toppled, their drivers were shot dead by daring soldiers who ran right up to them, or they simply stalled out from engine failure, rough terrain, or another mechanical issue. However, in the Nozo-Piikland battle of 1383, a trio of two leggers made a decisive difference in the fighting. Supported by infantry crews, a two legger charge with substantial firepower unleashed shattered Poumnian lines and drove the Poumnian position into a rout, eventually allowing the Jiishanâgi forces to push the Poumnians back to the Piik river. From this point on, a number of doctrinal observances became associated with two legger combat: infantry support, and charge/ram maneuvers, primarily as a means for breaking tough positions. They began to feature spiked ramming pieces or grates towards the front of their chassis for annihilating those in their way. The two legger also became a curious tool for the gendarmeries, its fearsome image and armored shell protected the officers and soldiers from restive citizenry, and it was used as a mobile base of operations for regional occupation.

The earlier two leggers featured primarily large, broad, metal wheels, which made for great agility in flat spaces, and long term reliability, requiring less maintenance, but also limited the size of the landship by weight, forcing engineers to install smaller artillery pieces and machine guns. However, the use of tracking for specialized mobile heavy artillery installations made for the possibility of designing two leggers with far greater firepower and armor. Treading also made them more resilient to irregular terrain in mountains and hilly settings. The first combat ready tracked Two Legger, "Baztakoi", Namanak Dodazh's "mobile fortress", was deployed late in the Nâgi-Poumnian war in 1386, and saw combat as a fortress buster in the scree ridden muddy hills of Pouromum.

The substantial increase in tonnage allowed by tracks allowed for not only a substantial increase in size and firepower in the design of traditional two leggers, but allowed for a substantial revision in design. The traditional steering cabin tower was moved to the center, but the engine brig was also expanded to include a crew quarters for carrying infantry, and the frontal artillery installations were expanded and improved. The "mobile fortress" of the later Nâgi-Poumian war was a fearsome installation on a strategic position in a battlefield, which came to be a central fixture of late fourteenth century and early fifteenth century warfare.

With the invention of larger and treaded two leggers, the heavy wear and tear on the treads, and more intensive engine usage made them less reliable, and oftentimes they would be towed by tractor to battle sites, rather than consistently driven across long distances, and supported by active infantry crews trained to fight alongside two leggers. The presence of regular support crews for larger two leggers led to their gradual adoption by the smaller two legger crews as well, in a limited way. Integration within infantry units trained to right two leggers helped deal with stability, and a ledge for sappers to rest on at the back of the two legger allowed for quick mobilization of duckboards and digging of gullies to traverse vastly irregular terrain in non-combat settings.

It is undoubtedly clear, declared Opau Ashkazh, in The Functional Account of Being (1302), a foundational text of the mechanist Ashkazhine epistemology and ontology, is that things exist because they do things, and what they do is the totality of their being. They are mere "machines" working on other machines. One cannot conceive of even the impression of an object save for the capacity of the object to act upon the mind. In such a way, the mind, the body, and all "things", the "thing" label now extended also to processes, words, and ideas, for these similarly have affective capacity, are merely acting and receiving machines, both affective and pathetic. This broadly synthetic and systematizing work would be followed by substantial revisions and elaborations by Ashkazh's students and Ashkazh himself, and would dominate the intellectual climate of Ishahfazh in the first half of the fourteenth century.

The posit of words as processes by which a subject acts, not as signifiers, gradually revolutionized the study of language. Drawing on the work of Ashkazhine functionalism and the parts of it devoted to philosophical and linguistic discourse, Ishagiza Bohdma in The Empirical Study of Word Usage and Translation (1320), gives a broad theoretical and ontological account of the functions of words and their systematic orderings as functional modes of speech, incorporating older notions of the grammarians such as the indicative and the imperative.

The advent of a linguistic paradigm that fully excluded any commitments to suppository or significatory features came to resurrect an old debate in metaphysics. Practically, argues, Rukroum Betz-Ohrun, in The Wallaby's* Tail (1315), an asemantic language fails to commit us to, not just categories or universals, but even particulars. A divergence from Ashkazhine functionalism, who believes we can talk of the machines that work, Betz-Ohrun and his school, drawing on a already restrictive epistemological system, came to believe that while words can be used to cause other to believe in entities, they do not actually speak of classes or entities or indicate classes or entities. *Meaning a large rodential creature found in Pruuntia.
Paternalistic attitudes have historically been popular in various parts of Ishafazhi society
French: patronage, lordship, bonds of social clientage, wala, etc. have been prevailing attitudes and implicit structural relationships that have ordered the relations between those considered social betters and social inferiors. Anti-Magisterial and Liberationist speculation broadly reinforced these ideas, either from a perspective of governmental responsibility for guaranteeing liberties, or, in a reactionary context, reaffirming the preferable relationship of lordly patronage as opposed to yeomanry and peasant freedom.

English: The speculation of the anti-magisterial movement led to a broad endorsement of rusticism and naturalism in political economy. Championing peasant agrarianism as "natural state of affairs" and particularist rural communitarianism as the perfect form of social organization, liberationist texts such as Dhov (Lord) Bozzamogga Nozkazh's Man and Nature and Madha Bidazh's Programme for the Shapt County Harvest popularized these political ideals. In many parts of the world the proliferation of these texts encouraged peasant militancy and regional organization, such as rural land banks, local assemblies, and a blending of the social and the political community in the countryside.

Liberationist and anti-magisterial speculation and political agitation broadly endorsed rural congregationalism as an ideal for the relationship between faith and social organization. Dencouning state involvement in ecclesiastical organization, political and religious activists beginning in the Gashdzii realms began to champion religious self-organization. Self-conscious religious organizations broadly had the effect of increasing social solidarity in regional communities, and reinforcing a sense of local and cultural identity.

Early liberationist writing implicitly lauded a certain sort of patriarchal masculine fraternity among the yeomen class, but later liberationist writers, notably Yathoon Ifo in An Enquiry into the Origins of Nations came to construe "fraternity", understood as an exclusive, ostensibly ultimately racial and brotherly, covenant of male yeomen who would fight, farm, and pray, autonomously but voluntarily together, as constituting the only legitimate foundation of nationhood. Extended so into the political sphere, "national fraternity" came to dominate the political discourse, especially in the revolutionary and free-yoker political contexts.

The Sovereign Will as an idealization of a resolved social covenant between voluntarily free citizens pooling their natural sovereignty endowed to them by nature, land-ownership, and strength ultimately became the rational basis for Liberationist governance. A tension in liberationist philosophy between the professed sovereignty of the individual, his (for ultimately the only political subject for the liberationist was a male) implicit relationship with the community, and the paradoxical need to construct a government to demarcate the limits of government always plagued liberationist speculation. These contradictions were ultimately resolved by Sevu Orooth in his influential synthesis Three forms of Mortal Governance, where, in the third part, he describes "the perfect [or divine - Sithevan makes no distinction] community" (Bo Yethu Anitoro), government by the sovereign will that preserves both communal liberty and individual liberty, both of which ultimately are free to then constitute a harmonized will by a self-conscious identification with its preserving faculties, the "benign circle' that is "the hand that holds itself", in Orooth's words.

The liberationist outburst stimulated the vigorous and self-conscious reformation and clarification of epistemological and practical principles by conservative and reactionary thinkers. Rallying behind the capacity for violence and naked force of reactionary armies, the clerical and municipal police, and the hangman's gallows, many defenders of the old order have come to champion the state's power to control as the foundation of its right to existence and right to command the lives of subjects. In the Modhag Police Commissioners Handbook of 1311, Arch Constable (Jakozzak) Vazzamak Nazakh lays out a plethora of methods for control of the populace, including closed juries, secret informants, penal labour colonies, mock-executions, and spectacular public violence, as well as provides short and practical justifications for the "maintenance of order and the foundations of the laws".

The context into which industrial society sprung was not an early modern context with a feeble public sphere, but a basically premodern cognitive context. The reactionary psychology was deeply rooted in ideas of personal servitude to a local master, whether the district governor of a Poumnian Inu (Imperial Province), the local Dhov (Lord) in the feudatories of Gashdiik, or the rootsman of the northern Tehurites. In a context of increasing literacy and political debate, in the 1310s and onward one sees a proliferation of public and private texts glorifying the romantic nation of service to another or the (exclusive) community
French: the bond between lord and master, comradeship in armies, and thrilling sublimity of adapting one's being entirely to the faithful service of a greater power. The gubernatorial oath of the Gozonazhk polity composed in about 1313 is a prime example of the adaption of romantic service to new context. Pledging strict loyalty, body and soul, the candidate is expected to prosecute his duties as governor of cities and provinces, "were he but a limb of the powers that be, the crown, estates, and parliament".

English: Self conscious and dogmatized parochialism gained currency as a political ideal in the early fourteenth century. Amenable to both the needs of Liberationists and Conservatives, ideological parochialism champions the immediate and the local, the family, the village, the court, the manor, as the natural organization of society. All political life is seen as the outgrowth of family life, and this is seen best kept as a small and local affair. Drawing on a vast collection of clerical and monarchical propaganda texts throughout history, the acme of this political development came with Dosh Modo of the Guzzadt Chruch in Gaub's The Care of Souls (1315), a synthetic work on the ways to goodness and salvation, which incorporates vast amounts of discourse on the role of the state, family, community, and the prince as the "little father", proxy of the mother Guzzadt, in a reality rife with religious order and significance.

The success of the Liberationist experiment in Sublime Veyethu after the revolution of 1297 planted a particular Vugiorian brand on Liberationist and Free Yoker discourse. Originally, of course, the Liberationist thought was an outgrowth of social-magisterialism, and the emphasis on freedom of congregational organization remained a cornerstone of Liberationist philosophy, but the Veyethian state took the extreme position of covering much of its political decisions with appeals to "natural theology", "the numinal will", and "the sacrosanct order". Even in non-vewugist contexts, Liberationist demands became intimately involved in, and made with appeal to, religious discourse and concepts.

A strange and short-lived doctrinal flourishing the Vokonazhi domains, Antietiologism was a fascination of the reclusive and esoteric literary intelligentsia. It emphasizes not the free will of all individuals, but specifically champions the senselessness of notions of cause, motion, behavior, and suggests that all action is both uncaused, and unwilled. Demanding a shift to the "psychology of the steppe", this being a period of fascination with the Hyundaatv of northern Bafozh, it attacks both the liberationist movement and conservatism positing an absence of meaning to both of their structures. Practically, it would encourage greater political disobedience and unorthodox thought in the academy. Its foundational text was Ishahmedes Doshkazhk's Will, Anti-Will, and Unwill (1322), a concise discourse on the concept of willing, and its ramifications in ethics, politics, and aesthetics. The reverberations of Antietiologism would be subtle but persistent, narrowly affecting political discourse, but spawning a degree of aesthetic and literary responses.

The advent of modern economic structures, increasing literacy, and the unorthodox liberationist employment of religious discourse encouraged a conceptual distinction between the city of god and the city of man. Once embedded in a common social habitus in most parts of the world, a key feature of the modern mind was this conceptual distinction and the possibility of the construction of secular subjecthood. Drawing on the work of various heterodox historical commentators on the matter, social thinkers and political dogmatists, such as Shomoho Mudt and Drid Tzau-Hydom began to advocate for a secular ideal. The secular impulse would undergird the demands for Statism and the formation of the Statist ideology.

Functionalist philosophy eventually found its way to the field of social and political speculation. In Shomoho Mudt's Social and Political Being (1319), Mudt declares there is nothing "given" about the state or the community save for that one of its functions is typically to perpetuate its own existence - a new, better state may be made by systems working within it, and the test of the state is merely its ability to "operate". Mudt's work would be foundational in the clarification of Statist political organization, as well as their revolutionary dogma.

The management of large populations always presents a challenge. “How to manage something as changeable and fickle as the crowd?”, asked Pazzak the Younger, in “Criminal Behavior in Grain Dole Recipients” (1325). Employing methods from the quantified social sciences, an emerging field of behavioral response study developed largely commissioned by civil servants and those with interests in public order. Eschewing psychological explanations as “impenetrable” or “unknowable” or “metaphysically unreal” (the functionalists), the Quantimetricians of the governments of Ishahfazh pioneered a number of incentive and disciplinary methodological guidebooks to both manage, guide, or gradually deconstruct social behaviors based on empirical outcomes.

Beyond the naked capacity for force, the so-called ‘civil elements’ are a near essential feature of those social organizations called states - a parasitic growth on tributary structures that has come to be a despotic and controlling organ. The rationalization and the improvement of the methodology and structure of the civilian bureaucracy can vastly increase the efficiency and strength of the fiscal-military institution that is the state. In the mid-fourteenth century, the synchronous expansion of the civil bureaucracy and the emergence of statist-functionalist philosophy stimulated a plethora of opinions on the improvement of the civil bureaucracy. Foremost among them was Goun Sha-Gosod Sha-Man’s “Treatise on Servility” (1326), which, while, cast in the strange context of the Poumnian divine cult, and the extension of divinity through service, clearly indicates a broad awareness of the importance of the development of a civilian ethos, a pride in employment, an identification with the state, and audit structures to ensure tireless labor in the service of the state. Particularly, Sha-Gosod Sha-Man’s emphasis on record keeping accountability and bypass appeals processes speaks to emerging notions of flexible bureaucracies that can purge their own calcified sinews.

The quick increase in direct administration of overseas possessions called for the development of techniques for managing foreign populations as well as flexible frontiers. Trial and error led to a gradual rationalization and formalization of methods, recorded and to be read by neophyte colonial functionaries, administrations, and officers. Summary executions, popular appeasements, maintaining segregated lands, granting of temple rights, integration with local elites, incentives to settle tribesmen, etc, all became systemic employments of the colonial governor.

The settlement of veterans of the imperial and metropolitan armies on the land of defeated peoples and states has always been a common practice of empires. In the imperial and colonial boom of the mid-fourteenth century, there was no exception. Veterans of all sorts, even sepoys from foreign continents, and indeed in some more populist governments, the poor and the wretched of the metropole, were often given “lots” of land, appropriated from the pre-colonial elites. Millions of hectares of land were used by these powerful landowners, who often employed local labour to build a new life in the colonies.

To belong to the imperial citizenship, especially in the colonies, is and was an object of cultural prestige, a certain status which is felt in all walks of life, positively, in the sense of opportunity, and negatively, in the sense of suffering avoided. Jobs, legal privileges, social privileges, and, for those more wretched, at least some sense of prestige and esteem. The social representation of belonging to the ruling cultural class of an empire often served to create a sense of social cohesion and encourage political pacificity, making the populace more tolerant of the actual burdens of empire, but in some degree expecting a return from it.

The encounter with underdeveloped and non-industrial peoples on a large scale, disseminated through the popular consciousness by increasing literacy and connectivity, helped drive a newfound awareness of civilisational differences, and sometimes, extreme cultural chauvinism. In “Report on three Urns from the Ouhrond, or, the Antiquities of Kovazh” (1338), the antiquarian and historian Ishamenes Moai classes the Auchobharr of the great Ourhond as a secondary-degree civilisation, in his developmental scheme, which he describes as “stultified and passive”. A sense of pervasive bigotry slowly emerged as a sense of superiority emerged in Ishahfazh, encouraging positive self-representations and loyalty to the metropolitan states claiming to represent a powerful, developed, imperial civilisation.

The process of expansionism and the commitment to it politically came by many reasons and with many justifications. Whether justified by the natural, quasi-functional expansion of organizational consuming systems, the higher civilisational quality of the imperial civilisation, or the casual appeal to force and might, in any case many people of Ishahfazh came to believe that military and territorial expansion was a natural and justified, legitimate process of states. The expansionist tendency, the promise of new land and new opportunities, served to often divert thoughts of social and political concern in the metropole.

The engagement with imperial thinking and imperial justifications prompted the periphery and the downtrodden, as well as the advantageous regionalist, to formulate an intellectual programme of active particularism. Resisting all forms of metropolitan domination, even in historically cosmopolitan imperial states, self-conscious particularism became a force to be reckoned with in the later half of the fourteenth century. The much glorified Dehuogi Haijduks, the bandit heroes half in the service of most noble house Budobaman, or the ferocious anti-imperialism of the Wushauw of the southern forests serve as prime examples of the will to resist centralisation and imperialism.

Boreal Flux, the strange illness that afflicts the northern realms, has long been a scourge to those unfamiliar with it. Spewing ghastly amounts of blood, causing hair loss, the body inflamed in rash and caked with necrotic skin, patients usually die a quick death. The discovery of the extremophile bacteria that cause this illness in the glacial streams of the northern lands in 1314 by Professor Huttag Gôhâgannud and his plan of inoculation for the Rannutan settlers in Paukzhodo allowed for the far safer settlement of these regions, as well as made military action in these regions easier.

I once was in Aekyum, yes. That was in the old days, the sleepy days, before the annexations. We’d come by ship, an old military packet, now in the hands of a captain who knew how to get past the lazy soldiers without needing to present papers. The sun was setting over the sea, and bathed the square, wooden spiked, sandstone tower of the teacher in a warm golden light. The fronds of the great trees swayed in the ocean breeze. We were on the edge of the old town. They said he kept an old midrash up there, and refused to see anyone, but now he was dying. I was his heir - distantly. Three flimsy old fools, wearing the flowing robes of the Shamushic cognoscenti, hissed instructions at me and shuffled me into the musty old fortress. There he lay, the windows boarded up, in stifling heat and stale air, the filthy room lit by a solitary candle. The old men left. He beckoned me to come towards the bed, weakly, but with a brittle insistence. There he discoursed on all matters of land and sea: he spoke of the Tuum-aeyl of old, he spoke of the world to come and the world gone by, he told of the teachings of Rod in his tower, the truth of extensions and passions, the mystery of the open mouth, the reason the serpent has no legs, and then he imparted to me the final secret, the last and only truth, the life work of the great mystic diviner Oton Betz-Oromon. I cannot tell you, but I will show you…

The functionalist impulse was vociferously responded to by the Naturalist school. Championing above all a posteriori reasoning, coherentist epistemology, and linguistic analysis ‘from the given’, it accepts both the semantic and pragmatic elements of language. It rejects the modus metaphysicis of the functionalists, suggesting that the functional analysis was ungrounded. In the “The Three Errors of the Sage of Gashdzoun” (1345) by Mruub Sha-Shum, the remarkable, sly and joyous “little thinker” of Prousorum, provides an elegant refutation of Azhkazine functionalism, and expounds, wittily, his system of Naturalist thought. Naturalism, while it enjoyed a brief intellectual vogue in the circles of Nozho and Pashdzii, was never embraced by its homeland of Poumnia, who’s religious traditionalism it was decidedly out of step with.

The clarification, and indeed sanction of, semantic theories in the naturalist system, paved the way for a system of semantic thought. Naturalist semantics took meanings as a given, and strove to clarify the relation between them and words. The most successful naturalist philosophy of language came from the enigmatic Ungoun Zaum-Morot of the Towuzhians. In The Unspoken Word, in particularly dense language and technical vocabulary, Zaum-Morot describes the immanent nature of meanings, and the subsistence of meaningfulness, particularly meaningful entities, as a consequence of the apparentness of communication. Zaum-Morot finds the ‘meaning’ token as a nexus of instantiation in the minds of the individuals speaking, and meanings to be the essential universals of presentation and information.

How does the world change? It doesn’t, said Uni Taujat, of the holy order of fighting monks in Unia: for it is ruled by Circles. For at least a millennium, the Monks of Unia have been driven mad by circles, though they’d tell you they’ve known the truth about circles since time began, which, according to them is never, so, they tell you, they’ve always known the secret of circles, because clearly they do now. Such mystic discourses were popularised in the publicist and anthropologist Izamobba Zevvoba’s The Shocking Testimonies of the Monks of Uni (1378), of which the primarily theme is the rules of Circles upon fate, upon time, and upon the lives of all. The vogue of pinning political developments and personal strife down to ‘temporal kyklocracy’, the rule of 'circles in time', became quite popular in southern Ishahfazh in the final quarter of the 14th century, a sort of reflex of the philosophical hack or the artistic dilettante.

The Functionalists of old found being in action and doing, the curricular determining of the machine. In Forward to thyself! (1373) Jêjor Yoguthâhu, the bastard son of a governor of colonial Paukzhodo, who inherited a large estate in the Rannutan heartland, declares the priority of essence to action and discourses upon through the modern miracles of the steam turbine and the machine gun. Somewhere in the tradition of Functionalism, he revives the language of Machines, but declares that the a-priori ‘reason of being’ is not defined as action is undergone, but the means of action are only defined by the vitalistic heart of a being. For Yoguthâhu, bafflingly, the essential steam turbine willed itself into existence, as that was one of the only ways it could find itself to exist. Similarly, the subject wills itself into being from pure essence, finding its ways of being fatalistically determined by its essential character.

What is the unintelligible utterance? Where is the unwritable proposition? Where is the private language? How does one speak of what is beyond language? Attacking all the sacred dogmas of Methodism, Vuiya bui'Tikamsho, the remarkable Bogoran exile in Pashdzii developed what he describes as aporetic pragmatics, what he declared to be, ‘the only way to rid ourselves of the trickery and snares of language’. Language, he acknowledges, as both a pragmatic and a semantic element, but this serves only to bewitch the senses. Only through acting upon the other through the conscious disentangling of the assumptions of language can we escape the tyranny of linguistic forms and communicate truth. The unutterable truths become a communicable paradigm through a broad collection of sincerely uttered falsehoods, contractions, and paradoxes. bui'Tikamsho never wrote a single book, but gave several discourses in Pashdzii to private audiences, and was briefly taken on as a lecturer in both Pashdzii and the Nozho, where his students took copious notes, during his floruit of 1381-1417.

The remarkable work of Taptnid Sha-Mang, the Poumnian Logician, Mathematician, and Linguist revolutionized language, mathematics, and logic by his ‘The Method’ (Gongum - 1345)  and ‘the Sign System’ (Tor Dromon - 1344). His extensive work in creating what he believed to be a self-consistent logical language that could speak of itself, and justify, itself paved the way for a rapid expansion of conceptual logics, linguistics and semiotics as a science, and even the aporetic metaphysics of Vuiya bui'Tikamsho in the end of the century.

Taptnid Sha-Mang’s ‘Gongum’, or the conceptual notation, would become the foundations of mathematical logic and seminotic notation for many years to come, artfully synthesizing early notions of quantified logic and propositional logic. It would later be criticized for its failure to treat identity as primitive, as well as its tolerance of universal statements with existential import.

Taptnid Sha-Mang’s works claimed to range over reality as a whole, and speak of everything, absolutely, transcending both functionalist nominalism and the ‘naive’ and borderline solipsistic views of the naturalists. Such a view influenced a certain grandiosity and authoritarian conservatism in thinkers immersed in Sha-Mang’s work.

The Methodist foundations ushered in a great blooming in Mathematical Philosophy, and the first coherent investigations into problems of the mathematical infinite, the reality of mathematical entities, and issues such as the interaction problem. The ‘Prousorum Circle’ under Sha-Mang’s successors and followers established an orthodoxy grounded in a broadly logicist scheme.

Swinery Raiders have for centuries been a fixture of warfare in Ishahfazh. The vast plains of Gashdziik in the west and the Sithevan lands of the east encourage robust swinery as essential to warfare. The ‘raider’ unit became a recognizable soldier in the early 9th century, an armoured swinery soldier, trained in hand to hand combat, as well as shooting with light arquebus. A descendant of the aristocratic swinery of old, this unit carriest to some extent the greatest prestige, even though the actual usefulness of mounted and armed swordsmen has declined.

Swinery Lancers are the lightest and most flexible of the three ‘modern’ swinery units. Emerging as a typical unit somewhere in the 10th century, it is believed in the uplands of Vafaut after the style of the local mounted warriors who used pistols and billhooks to defend and raid, the ‘lancer’ is equipped with a long lance and light pistol-style firearms. They typically are employed to engage in close-quarters melees, and have small ‘upland’ bred Vafauti hogs as their mounts.

Swinery Gunners are the most flexible and standard of the ‘big three’ of the modern swinery unit. This is broadly a catch-all term for mounted soldiers armed with sabers and light carbines used in skirmishing, scouting, civilian management, and open battle. Usually mounted on East Vokonazhi chargers, their mounts tend to be fast but unwieldy and ferocious.

The extension of the Functionalist principle to the realm of bodies and the body social spawned ostensibly one of the most profound results of the 14th century, that of the Biomachinal analysis of species. The fundamental insight is that reproduction is a functional value of successful machines, and that more successful machines reproduce more, that this becomes a new domain for competition, and thus changes accrue. The biological machine is just this
French: a self-replicating machine that resists disintegration. The insights of Adunnô Vôhannud, the Rannutan aristocrat and natural scientist, led him to publish the world renowned Machinic Success and The Principle of Differentiation (1343) essentially summed up the principle, where he declares ‘I must conclude that those creatures which contained those most suitable features are those ones that are passed on, and so in fact gradually speciate and define the biomachine.’.

English: The absolutist impulse is a radical reformulation and indeed clarification of the purpose and even very being of the state
French: the state should be seen as an enterprise that succeeds or fails in the preservation and expansion of its own power, capacity, and efficiency, and nothing else - as an entity that lives, breathes, and grows for its own sake. The individual must be absolutely subordinated to the functions of the state, to ultimately become little but an appendage of the state. The Nâgi theorist Pazzak Moggadazh III, writing in 1367 in ‘Society and the State’ suggests that ultimately ‘society’ is an outgrowth of the state. Only the state has the regulating principles to even give order to such a thing as a society, and even primitive tribes exist socially in virtue of their political existence. Fusing Biomachinic elements with an extreme form of Statism, the more popular ‘Absolutist Manifesto’ or ‘Notes of The Monsoon Speech to the Delegates of the 23rd Nâgi Statist Party Congress’ of 1369, Moggadazh called for the state, famously, to take ‘absolute precedence’ and for the state to prosecute its struggle against the combined forces of the northern alliance and the Poumnians to an absolute degree. This would lead ultimately to a split between the statists and the so-called-absolutists, and the foundation of the first Absolutist party in the great Nâg.

English: Absolutist Party organisation typically proceeds by binding democratic centralist principles. The party line must be kept absolutely once a resolution is agreed upon. In the notes from the 4th Pan-Nâgine Absolutist Party Congress of 1383, one finds as an example delegate Bida Gamat denounced fellow party member Modanak Vazzunak for ‘defeatism’, ‘conspiracy’, and for leading a Poumnian sponsored terrorist cell of ‘disgraced Gazzapt-Kozzite autonomists’, and Vazzunak was duly expelled for his non-party thought. The charges of defeatism and conspiracy were later proven false, but his membership of the party remained revoked due to his repeated autonomist advocacy.

The formation and governmental power of a number of absolutist parties, especially in the Great Nâg territories in the late fourteenth century allowed for an absolutist political culture to flourish and develop a number of further principled elaborations of their theory and practice. Orthodox Absolutism follows the teachings of Pazzak III and his disciple Bida Gamat. The ‘Foftaptan Nâg Bazd’, or the ‘Investigative Concerns Board’ of the Nâgine state carried wide discretionary powers of arbitrary detainment, torture and execution, as well as encouraged a culture of peer-denunication and informancy. The notorious FNB became a model for the intelligence, secret police, and plainclothes gendarmes of many absolutist states.

The first Theocratist paramilitary group was that of Deacon Mogga, the totalitarian preacher of the settler communities of the Gozonazh peninsula. Forming an alliance with great castellans on the frontier in the late 1330s, the theocratists bands became a terrorizing force, massacring recalcitrant workers and peasants, committing wanton acts of violence against the Vuyti ethnic minority, and exercising influence over local organs of the state. The Theocratist paramilitary group became the paradigmatic way in which theocratists came to power, an alliance of dissident clerics, the disaffected soldiery, and wealthy conservative extremists.

The movement by Theocratists such as Deacon Mogga to found an ostensibly political engaged party to engage in regular politics alongside their violent paramilitary groups paved the way for their engagement with the political masses both through terror and through rhetorical demagoguery. The paradigmatic theocratist party aims to seize power by legitimate or illegitimate means and then transform the state into a theocratist dictatorship.

A ‘brigand’ was a colloquial name for any packet ship or commercial vessel that was retrofitted with plating and higher-caliber cannons. They rely on their light speed to harass enemy transports and shipping. Maritime Brigandage saw much action in the Jiishanâgi-Poumnian war of 1324-8.

A ‘pitpot’ is a general term for any sea-going vessel that is built entirely of steel and without any timber. Their sturdy hulls help them avoid dangerous artillery from other ships. The first pitpot was the Pride of Nozho, constructed by Jiishanâgi engineers in 1309. It was sunk in 1325 in a war with the Poumnians.

A ‘Bibbler’ is a general term for covered-deck steel built seagoing vessels that reached a certain tonnage and maximum speed. Deck-coverings allowed for better armouring, the ability to brave more stormy waters, and general resistance. Sitting lower in the water than Pitpots or Crackwhips, they are said to ‘bibble’ as the hum of the engine stirs the surrounding waters.

Crackwhips were large, fast steel-plated ships with large cannons. Advances in engine technology allowed for substantially increased gun-sizes and vessel speeds on deck-ships. The first Crackwhip-class (really, Shroukshou-class) ship was the ‘FWV Shroukshou’ built by the Sha-Gosod Works in Kuuwumn. This formidable ship has one of the most legendary records in naval history, engaged in multiple hundreds of naval combats and said to have sank over 70+ proper enemy vessels.

Substantial increase in engine power around this time also allowed for the construction of massive vessels, commonly called ‘sea-forts', equipped with high caliber guns, and designed to slowly cruise around, patrolling waters and projecting power. With over 10,000 tons of displacement, the “Oknapt” of the Nâgine forces, commissioned in 1355 was at its time the largest ship sailing, and described as an ‘unsinkable Sea-Fort’.

The ‘FWV Pudwou’, the pride of the Poumnian navy, became synonmous with a class of super large battleship reaching displacements of over 20,000 tons and with certain gun-configurations. Larger and more resilient than the already superlative laden sea-forts, The Pudwou launched an era of naval panic.
Torpedo Boats are cheap and numerous. They are equipped with Torpedoes to attack bigger ships like Crackwhips and Sea-Forts.

By the mid 1390s, cruisers had specialised into a role of long-distance stalking, and hunting smaller ships. Covered Crackwhip models allowed for combat in the stormy far seas, and long-distance maneuverability.

Advances in hydranautic design in the 1390s and onward made for some of the most streamlined hulls yet. Firms like the Sha-Gosod works and their engineers designed crackwhips that could cut through stormy and choppy waters with record speeds.

The 1390s and the 1400s also featured innovations in large ships and capital ships. New hulls and defensive techniques, such as better plating below the waterline, undersea beta-boats for torpedo defense, and aircraft defenses made modern capital ships more formidable than ever.
The transition to oil-based ships drastically improved efficiency, and allowed for less needless ballast on the ship.

One of the greatest of the second wave of economic speculation, Dozmenes Miibziva of Nozho in Jiishanâg was the first to suggest that Jiishanâg’s economic preeminence was due to its role as the congress point of world markets. In ‘Thick and Thin Markets’ (1304), Miibziva suggested that for many centuries economic development languished because of technological and political limitations to markets. He suggested that large empires like Kiidnazh facilitated a great degree of economic development, and preserved technological knowledge, but it wasn’t until world spanning trade networks projected by the Jiishanâgi and Poumnian states concentrated markets that it became incentivized for artisans and engineers to explore industrialising.

Voun Sha-Pomid, of the little known Pomid family, distinguished himself by his ‘state’ based criticism of early economic orthodoxy established in the late 1200s by the ‘classical’ Gashdzii economists. Rather than a reified ‘economy’ that stands somehow aloof from the state (or even ‘society’), presaging the statists, Sha-Pomid suggested the economy exists in virtue of, and is driven by, ultimately, the organisation of the state, and only the expansion of states and their services serves to grow industry.

Gizshaug Pâshodazhi is most famous for defending the orthodox ‘consumption’ theory of economic growth in the ‘demand’ pamphlet wars of the early fourteenth century. He suggested that growth was largely driven by demand, particularly luxury demand, and advocated principally for the lowering of taxes on the rich.
The invention of the first motor car by Mifazh Padud in Bagh, 1357 was a cause of mild interest for the rural rich, at the time, and took very many years before it entered pratical service.
The engineers of the Padud firm redoubled their prestige by being the first to invent the first airgoing vessel in 1375. Its maiden voyage crash near the old 'holy mountain in the Paguyti lands.

The first common way to transmit electricity was direct current or DC, where the electrons flow in only one direction. Batteries produce direct current and it is commonly used in applications requiring low voltages. High voltage direct current is used to transmit power to long distances, especially when using underwater cables and to run trains.

In alternating current or AC systems electrons flow in both directions in wave patterns. Those in the Great Nâg were some of the first to pioneer the use of alternating current, which quickly became standard for large industrial or military projects.

The polyphase system is a way to help transmit alternating current efficiently. In it two or more phases travel simultaneously. In industrial applications three waves is the standards, although at first two phases were used.
Mohdhâgazh Paup, the 'Baron of the Cloth', sponsored the developement and factory organisation of his in-house power loom, which revolutionised production of cloth.
The Guzzamak Mule was the most popular spinning mule in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.
Vazumedan needles allowed for most mules and spinning machines to handle more fine cloth, a large improvement on the earlier Mule
Ashnuz Gozomak's wheel powered motor-reaper vastly increased agriculutral yeilds.
Nuzhamedes of Oazud, by an ingenious system of grinding pegs, invented a machine for fast and efficient threshing.
The Nascent Sha-Ashouw firm pioneered standard gauges of small weaponry due to their contracts with the Poumnian government. The machines for producing these parts were widely copied.
Research into industrial efficient by the economists of the Great Nâg's absolutist secrateriate produced a remarkable ammount of innovations, most notably line-work style organisation.
Dhuchâ Kazh was the first to invent his 'steel lungs' for bubbling oxygen through molten iron to process it into steel and funneling out slag.

Lung style steel was limited to steel with much too much phosphorous. The 'Great Oven Style', pioneered by the engineers of the state-backed Sha-Ashouw firm, pioneered the Great-Oven style superheat iron and create steel.

The invention of coatings to protect against reactions with Phosophous were pioneered in the mid 1320s and allowed for those dependent on Kazh or Lung steel to catch up with those casting Great-Oven style steel.

The first vaccination was pioneered by Shumid Sha-Munpt, the Poumnian commander of Mra-Ouswun. Observing Qooxibi habits in exposing their children to the flies at night, he realised that moderate illnesses could be prevented by stimulating the immune system. In 1298 he suggested using Swine-Flu, a relative of the ghastly nocceus torpicus bacterium that devestated populations, in safe innoculations. This method meant that one could immunize animals and hominids from illnesses that flourished. This made life easier for man, cattle and thrall tending more profitable.

Adunnô Vôhannud, the great bioneer of the Biomachinal thesis, also innaugerated the study of heritible traits in his pioneering research on the populations of fat, large flying insects that produced a common tasty egg, which he bred on his great estate. These principles allowed for the greatly increased succesful breeding of livestock animals.

This marked the beginning of a new field of science and technology  - biotechnology. Research sponsored by the Vokonozhi thick-swine cartels combined fermentative processes (enzymatic hydrolization) with a thermodynamic process (catalytic hydrogenation). One result of this combination was margarine, which greatly improved the supply of the population with essential unsaturated fatty acids.
The classic filament bulb of the 1360s became a cheap and convient way of lighting the world, allowing work and leasiure to go on for longer, and at a lower cost than the gas lamps of earlier times.

The discovery and design of beautiful, soft gas lighting freed the hominid from the tyrany of day and night and illuminated the cities and estates of the civilised world. Softly glowing laterns now line boulevards, wealthy houseowners light their fine living rooms, scholars pour over texts late into the night, and the factory is now lit late with soft glowing lights.

Yaksau Pojar Sem Moswie, the Takemogine inventor, was the first to invent a device for transmitting sound across distances through electricity, by pioneering the correct manner of producing current between two diaphrams. He and his sons became quite wealthy through their business.

When motor-cars had started to gain popularity on the roads, it did not take long for more innovative engineers to find a way to begin replacing swine in the fields. Early experiments with steam-powered farm machinery had failed, but lighter combustion engines revolutionised farm work.
From pulpin woods, a a form of synthetic spindleweed was developed in the late 1390s. This was a widely popular consumer product.
Plastics expiriments in the 1390s yeilded some of the first consumer and industrial plastics, driving both industry and plantation in Bafozh.

The vacuum tube (also known as the thermionic valve) is a device that utilizes the flow of current through a vacuum. In a vacuum tube electrons travel via thermionic emission from a hot filament (negative cathode) through the vacuum to a positive electrode (the anode). Additional electrodes were later interposed between the anode and cathode, enabling amplification and switching of signals.

Masogu Hahab-So, a civic minded citizen of the Veyethun regime, in the 1304 invented a useful form of seed drill, which he billed as invented specifically for public usage and for the agrarian good. Pulled by Swine-Mule, the Veyethun revolutionary government actually established a number of workshops for the production of these tools and distrubted them to local villages.
The gradual transition to iron-based farming equipment by advances in metallurgy encouraged clever designs and made plowing fields far easier.

The telephone switchboard is a system of electrical components used to connect telephone calls. In Poumnia, these were often worked by slaves in sweltering conditions, and in the Great Nâg, by detainees of the absolutist regime.

At this points the trenches grew to formidable systems of trenches with two or even three lines of defenses bolstered by concrete fortifications and machine gun positions. The protracted wars between the Great Nâg and the Poumnian regime made the lands of Dhuknâg into a veritable labyrinth of trenches.

After the end of the grinding Poumnian-Nâgine conflict and its attendant regional conflicts, the major powers had to re-evaluate their military strategies in light of the brutal lessons learned during the years of inconclusive trench warfare. One major school of thought that emerged focused on the importance of using massed firepower, principally in the form of artillery, to overwhelm the enemy and literally blast a hole in their lines to facilitate an advance, while another school of thought suggested that the key to victory on the modern battlefield was mobility, so that friendly forces could maneuver around enemy strongpoints to pursue the attack on more advantageous terms.

After the Poumnian-Nâgine war, many nations' armies kept evolving in nature and focus. A greater degree of motorisation, with mass availability of cars and trucks, added to the ever-changing nature of land units across the globe.

With the mass casulaties suffered in the Poumnian-Nâgine war, and the dawning of the motorised age, traditional swinery was on its way out. The new focus on motorisation changed the way swinery was to be used, and its role on the battlefield. No longer swine-mounted, soldiers would be mounted instead on motorised vehicles. Motorisation would also allow for more fire power from heavier guns, and speed up deployment times.

As experience from the Poumnian-Nâgine demonstrated, infantry units, especially those operating in rough terrain, needed a viable option for increased fire power. Traditional guns were too heavy, and too bulky to be used effectively or moved rapidly in adverse conditions. Shorter range guns of smaller calibers, which were easily moved by horse, vehicle, or manpower, were developed to fill this need.

Coming out of the mold of traditional artillery, combined with the experiences of the Poumnian-Nâgine War and the rapid increase in motorisation, the medium artillery gun was developed. Of modest calibers, these guns were the standard for regular infantry units, providing them with a greater fire power capability and mobility that they had previously lacked.

Introduced at the beginning of the 11th century, the flintlock rapidly replaced earlier firearm-ignition technologies, such as the doglock, matchlock, and wheellock mechanisms. It continued to be in common use for over two centuries, replaced by percussion cap and, later, cartridge-based systems in the late thirteenth and early foruteenth century. Although long superseded by modern firearms, flintlock weapons enjoy continuing popularity with black-powder shooting enthusiasts.
A muzzle-loading rifle is a gun in which the projectile and propelling charge is loaded through the front-end of the gun, in contrast to a breech loading rifle.

A breech-loading weapon is a firearm in which the cartridge or shell is inserted or loaded into a chamber integral to the rear portion of a barrel. Although breech-loading weapons were developed as far back as the late 9th century, breech-loading became more successful with improvements in precision engineering and machining in the fourteenth century.

Bolt action is a type of firearm action in which the weapon's bolt is operated manually by the opening and closing of the breech (barrel) with a small handle. The first bolt-action rifle was produced in 1295 by Chyoosh Gooth-so, brother of the famous Veyethun revolutionary, following work on breechloading rifles. Ishahfazhi armies continued to develop bolt-action rifles through the latter half of the fourteenth century, and the Poumnian-Nâgine War marked the height of the bolt-action rifle's use, with all of the nations in that war fielding troops armed with various bolt-action designs.

The first machine gun was pioneered by Vodid Protum, a 'monk' in the Poumnian imperial clergy and civil service. Trained as an engineer by the Sha-Shoummid firm, he later became a minor apendage to a colonial military garrison to interface between the local community and the military fortress, where he enjoyed much leasiure to tinker. In 1337 he returned to the Shoummid plants and later came to design a 'spinning', rapid fire gun. The Sha-Shoumid firm later became premier manufacturer of self-turning machine guns, invaluable to Poumnian colonial interests.

The advent of mass literature changed the relationship between texts and culture greatly. No longer the preserve of the elite, anyone from the working man on the streets and even the colonial exile was able to, and indeed wanted to, read and learn. A great amount of the new reading material was so-called ‘pulp’, made from cheap wood-pulp or recycled papers, and usually printed bawdy tales, seditious material, revolutionary speculation, daily almanacs, horoscopes, etc.

The discovery of electromagnetic radiation and its possible use for transmitting voices was largely employed first by the state to disseminate propaganda, but soon become also an outlet for popular dissatisfaction.

Audiocinematric techniques were immediately identified as hazardous by most regimes, from the Nâgine Secretariate to the Poumnian autocracy. It was primarily first employed for the purposes of patriotic education for the masses, but to some extent as well served to democratise culture.

The development of the Biomachinical principle was extended to the world of societies and ‘races’ quite easily. Competition became the order of the day, and the weak at home and abroad were expected to die by the wayside, pruned from the family of the living by nature’s prudential machinic order. Bodmha Damaz, the North Gashdzii agitator, shortly after having read the works of Adunnô Vôhannud, in 1347  proclaimed a need for ‘unending war’ against the foreigner, to temper the steel of the Gashdzii race, and suggested that should the Gashdzii in fact cease their imperial aims, the configuration of their own society will become progressively weaker. A craze for eugenic societies, eugenic laws and war followed.

An important development in naval warfare in the early-15th century was the wireless, or radio communications. This allowed naval headquarters to communicate with fleets at sea in order to give updated orders, and also allowed admirals to communicate much more effectively with individual warships in their fleets, in comparison with older methods such as signal flags. However, one drawback of wireless was that it was also possible for the enemy to listen in on wireless communications, and soon the major navies would establish organizations to glean valuable intelligence from enemy communications.

The use of war games to plan and prepare for war is as old as warfare itself: the ancient Poumnian game of Prak is a testimony to this. However, serious analytical naval war gaming emerged in the late 14th and early 15th centuries. Major naval powers would use detailed gaming systems that took account of such variables as a ship's armour, speed, and the number and caliber of guns in order to determine battle damage and the ultimate victor. These naval war games were used to test strategic plans, and different means of countering potential enemy strategies and warships.

In the aftermath of the Poumnian-Nâgine war, the major powers put an increasing emphasis on what came to be known as combined operations. This represented the utilization of land, sea, and air forces together to achieve a single strategic objective. Often revolving around amphibious operations, combined operations often fit within larger naval strategic objectives, including the destruction of enemy naval assets and the securing of sealanes. No longer could navies operate in isolation from the other branches of the military, and the development of new tactics was required to integrate naval warfare into the larger strategic perspective.

The old naval codes of the past were brutal, and harsh, and gave naval life its fearsome name. Modern naval codes are not much different, especially in the Miiv's more authoritarian states, but more optimised to incentivise obedient behaviour from seamen.

In the North of Ishahfazh, the water is wide, and especially states like the Takomogine Monarchy developed a need to project influence into distant waters. This meant building navies with resilient hulls and long-distant capability.

In the south of Ishahfazh, on the Zhibomgid sea, there was a constant need to project influence and control these highly contested waters. This meant that size and firepower was prized above all, at the cost of reliability, given that ships could quickly repair at major dockyards or shelter in colonial harbours.

As more individuals became involved in investing in securities markets in the early fifteenth century, the practice of buying on margin developed to increase the amount of shares that could be bought with minimal initial overhead. The principal of buying on margin is that if the investment makes a profit, the profit would cover the cost of the commission charged for allowing the purchase of large amounts of securities with only a minimal initial investment. The risk involved in this type of investment is that if the investment shows a loss, the difference between the initial investment and the commission charged for the purchase must be made up by the investor. How low an initial margin was prudent for the securities industry to accept would be the subject of intense debate, as lower margins both allowed investors with limited capital to invest in markets, but raised the risk of default by these limited-capital investors should the investments fail to produce profits

The advent of the machine gun made colonial ‘negotiations’ and the control of native populations far easier. Armed with vastly superior technology of Sha-Asahouw Automatic Rotary Guns, at a number of key battles in the colonial scramble for Bafozh, Ishahfazhi soldiers made swift work of large groups of natives, whether armed or civilian.

By an effort to elevate by means of science and reason the state to the authoritarian steward, and manager, of all things, both man and nature, all in the service of the archepiscops of prince, the modern reactionary state became exceedingly efficient in managing society. A proliferation of directives issued by governing authorities and regional governments in Vokonazh at this time are an excellent testimony to this. The segregation of dining areas for state serfs and slaves, the proliferation of secret policing, regularised methods of informing, the quantification of man, nature, industrial and agricultural yields have all left a proliferation of bureaucratic records.

Around this time, states increasingly began normalising and reducing the impact of the process of mass-mobilisation with the expectation of forced labour on behalf of citizens. War offices and district military authorities were issued with the right to force citizens to work off-hours in state munitions plants, compelling aristocrats to share serfs or slaves with the state. Even states reputed as more ‘gentle’ began to endorse this practice. In a particularly stark example, the Gaubjan courts ruled in 1344 that those who were not drafted or serving were in fact criminally liable if they failed to answer to the ‘labour draft’ at the munitions plant.

It has long been a truth that certain species seem more suitable for certain roles - the quick witted Sapinoids have always excelled as artisans, and the giant Occidental Gigantoids, or the Byotrin, have made fearsome warriors. Around this time, the practice of institutionalizing speciated differences in both occupational employment and military service served to further stratify society, and breed enmity between states of different species. An excellent example of this is a Vafauti directive from 1343, directing the organisation of a battalion of Shagmodt ‘war-slaves’ from Qir, to be employed against the Shuknazhi, in hopes that the mountain giants would terrify them.

The wave of Theocratist speculation also stimulated pure reactionary nostalgia. Rather than challenging the rise of the state with a modernised reactionary, nostalgic romanticism called openly for a barbarous return to the age of the squires, lords, and primitive violence. Gibbalobba, that Dhamapahan adventurer, most famous for his great raid on mount Femooru in the Guth-Gabob, in his later years became a famous writer on these matters, producing a great many quasi-metaphysical tracts on the ‘soul of the nation’, as well as dubious histories of the ancient Gashdzii, their emperors, princes, and generals.

The institutionalism of meritocratic elitism, where the army, church, academy, and conservative circles formed a closed unit wherein a promising youth, with conservative principles could earn a secure role in the bureaucracy or army, served to ossify the structures of the state into a monolithic and secure organ of reaction. In the Vokonazh of the 1350s-70s, the ‘constabulary’, as the forces of reaction had always been known, increasingly came to recruit and induct rural youths of talent, strengthening its capacities and quelling any possibilities of resentment by integrating them into the institutional structure. One such example is Kazzamenes Padud, from rural Pava province, one of the first chiefs of police in Modhag (from 1357) without an aristocratic background. He was of course ennobled, later.

A true science of significance did not arrive until the 1350s. Mruub Sha-Ibu (not the general, but a relative of a minor line of house Ibu) was the first to formulate a unified doctrine of signs, both natural and unnatural, and an account of the interrelation between the mind and the grasping of the meaning of smoke, a character, and an utterance. His multivolume work ‘A systematic investigation into the character of informative processes’ (1358) long became the established reference for the concerns of semiotics and significance.

The flourishing of logical systems in the methodist paradigm eventually bloomed into the metaphysical investigation of reference, and referential utterances. The so-called ‘Green School’, in the Guzzadt Seminary in Gaub developed a remarkable repertoire of forms of reference, and speculative metaphysical consequences.

Wood is composed of cellulose fibres that are cemented together with a substance called lignin. To transform wood into pulp, the fibres must be separated, either by a mechanical or chemical process. This technology helped to saturate the ever growing hunger for paper of the 14th century printing industry.

A concentrated impulse to an autonomous social sciences finally emerged in the mid 1340s, distinct from academic psychology and from social management by the state. Institutions came to define departments, methodologies, and orthodoxies, largely drawing on the Methodist and Naturalist philosophies, opposed to the metaphysical functionalism of the Pazzak circle and his followers.

A comprehensive study of folk and social repertoires of behaviour was a key ambition of certain circles of the sociometric milieu. Mozzak Midadazh’s famous ‘Acculturation and Social Signs’ (1347) paved the way for the semioticians, the mirror-theorists, and the later gestalt theory. In the book, he describes his theories of a formation of an inner world through the other, and the proliferation of social rituals in the construction of the actual reality of the individual.

The growth of the social sciences as an autonomous academic institution, rather than a mere tool of social control, ushered in a proliferation of social speculation about choice and crowd behaviour. Drawing on the schools and writings of the behaviour Quantimetricians, the Action Quantimetricians attempted to systemise a total account of behaviour and the motivational systems involved.

The 1340s witnessed, as well as a proliferation of the social sciences, a great enthusiasm for anthropological collection and classification. Melding with notions of civilisational quanta, the famous ‘anthropological exhibitions’ of captured bafinoids, azuroids, and giganoids were exhibited to a fascinated Ishahfazhi public, who read as well the proliferation of studies of cranial structures, social and fertility rituals between cultures and peoples, and a general fanatical need to classify, collect, order, and rank the species and cultures of the world.

The proliferation of social-psychological thought in the late 14th century drove a fanatical interest by the state not just to control and manipulate social behaviour, but acculturate subjects into a manner of being that was entirely sympathetic to the state. Midadazh’s theories of acculturation were extended by Urunt Betz-Thon, the pioneer of the Gestalt theory, into a belief that patterns of being or subjectivity could be established comprising largely divorced concerns, and that disparate needs and feelings could be synthesized, by clever presentation and acculturation, into a desired experience. The FNB of the Nâgine absolutist state eagerly attempted to mould its soldiers into undesiring killing machines by progressive deprivation of attachment to family supplemented by persistent subliminal exposures to messaging that stated their needs were being acknowledged.

Increased state interest in control of the subjective experience of the subject, and explicit and acknowledged bids to cultivate this drove, as to be expected, a school of cognitive resistance inspired by the antietiologists of Vokonazh in the first quarter of the century. Exhorting the subject to develop ‘parallel social networks’ and to engage in meaningless acts of destruction, insubordination, and terror, the ‘new antietiologist’ movement existed as a radical and underground fringe of the Nâgine intelligentsia. Distributed in underground meetings in filthy tenements, or in abandoned soldiers' dugouts, hod-podge, bricolage texts, reprinted in inconsistent and apocryphal collections such as ‘the red and white book’, and ‘three cheers for my lovely aunt!’ became the essential substance matter of the movement

By abolishing non-standardized and strange divisions of the currency like mohaks and thrall-coins, and only having a decimal system such as the one in the Veyethun State (1 Veyethun Tho = 100 v'ath), the everyday usage of money was simplified.

The dramatic pressures of governing a late fourteenth century state often drove desperate politicians to take their countries off the gold standard and issue copious amounts of bills to fund debt, the army, and social services.

At this point combinations of producers and consumers, in conjunction with the customs offices of the state, developed for efficient means by they could certify legitimate goods at customs and in factory/mercantile inspections, guaranteeing higher quality inputs for producers

The eugenics craze stimulated by the sociomachinic princple encouraged certain states, those who still tollerated anthropic chattel, to allow the purposeful breeding of workers, by selecting certain species, and traits, and raising the offspring entirely with a mind that they would work in a firm, firms managed to equip themselves with anthropic property with a high capital value.
