In more progressive states, the concern still found a home in biological aptitude testing and species oriented hiring pratices.

At this point, a coherent science of management emerged. Drawing togther their various antecedents of beatings, bonus-incentives, work-specialisation principles, a management culture developed that involved the scientific study of productivity, motivation, and task-completion quality.

Industrial growth created a demand for nearly every sort of product, including by-products. Coking, for examples, produced tar and ammonia, which were highly prized by the chemicals industry. A consciousness of a by-product market produced additional profits for the plant and stimulated production.

Industrial growth, improved medicine, and urbanisation stimulated the growth of large, concentrated consumer and producer networks. An avaliability of both inputs and markets encourged continous production, increasing throughput and specialisation.

The germ theory of disease states that some diseases are caused by microorganisms. These small organisms, too small to see without magnification, invade humans, animals, and other living hosts. Their growth and reproduction within their hosts can cause a disease. The germ theory was proposed in the mid-6th century and gained widespread credence when substantiated by scientific discoveries of the 12th through the late 14th century. It supplanted earlier explanations for disease, such as the Bog-Miasma theory of the Poumnians, who happened to be misguided by the patches of toxic gaseous spore buildup that occured in their fungalised swamplands.

By providing quotas of expected military consumption well in advance of military expansion and indeed usage of materiel during war to large industrial firms, the state aided producers by producing market security and driving secure investments.

By means of an 'open door' between industry and the political and financial sectors, producers were able to secure favourable laws, and the government was able to secure to stimulation of what were deemed essential industries. By not just granting cartelisation permissions, but proactively mandating them, the government could ensure growth in critical sectors with the consent of the economic elite.
By granting certain firms permission to organise into market-controlling cartelised groups, industries could be saved from depression and failure.

Efforts by statesmen at this time were oriented around securing markets for excess capital investment, as well as markets for industrial goods and those for raw resources, and organising them into a self-perserving organic system by means of protective tariffs on goods from beyond the imperial system. Empire and Tariff went happily together, subdiving the world into a collection of increasingly autonomous imperial systems.

A mark of a self-sufficient and robust state-economy-complex was the ability to survive market disruptions, blockades, and emargos, especially with regards to military goods. Synthetic oil refineries, driven by economic necessity, were key to this.

A major hallmark of the modern fiscal state in the 14th century was its ability to raise massive amounts of cash for the purposes of waging unending war. Continous issuing of long-term government bonds to large sections of a marketised public, and the large scale embrace of purchasing these mechanisms by the public, allowed states to raise ever larger sums.
A major way in which the 14th century state built trust in the financial system was a well-publised sinking fund for debt. This created trust in the government's ability to pay off accumulated debts.

Traditional Methods of tax collection: inquisitorial methods and the reliance on trust and lay commisioners slowly gave way in the 14th century, facilitated by the gradual melding of state and industry into a military-industrial complex, into large scale investigation of private incomes at source through the cooperation of industrial firms. This enabled the government to raise even larger revenues and float even larger bonds.

In the late 14th century, close collaboration between cartels, the financial sector, and the military officialdom facilitated broad trust by industrial and financial elites in subscribing to and supporting government military intiatives and spending. Especially, the Sha-Shoummid firm was closely involved in Imperial Memoranda on the post-war settlement of the Poumnian Nâgine war, advocating for the total conversion of the peripheral Gashdzii states of Vafaut and Dhamapaha, which were aligned with the Nâg, into a Poumnian friendly 'coal field', and to deprive the Nâgine firms of their access to friendly and nearby coal and iron reserves.

Pastoralism was basically an aesthetical reflection of the liberationist movement, lauding the virtues of the argicultural, free, male community. Pastoralist Literature typically took the form of odes and peans to country life. Particularly notable pastoralist poets were Chyush Goosh-so, Vazzunak Buzfa, and Qip Quam Ghech.

Pastoralism was basically an aesthetical reflection of the liberationist movement, lauding the virtues of the argicultural, free, male community. High pastoralist music was largely an adapation of folk melodies, set to grand chambers, and performed usually in the Veyethun chamber of deputies. Notable composers were Vyit Gat-so and Mozza Chaptazh.

Pastoralism was basically an aesthetical reflection of the liberationist movement, lauding the virtues of the argicultural, free, male community. Pastoralist art took the form of typically bucolic scenes, as well as folk-inspired sculpture. Notable figures were Yith Chum-so and Mazzak Padudazh

Symbolist was a popular art movement in the early part of the 14th century. Connected vaguely to the reactionary movement at the time, it was steeped in mannered echos of tradition, religious imagery, and ancient cultural symbols. Symbolist literature typically took the form of allegorical fables rooted in the mythic past, or long, complex novels echoing annalistic systles, reminsicent of cosmic drama. Notable authors include Wudwou Sha-Mosod, Vyith Gum-so, and Yaukz ApOswieg.

Symbolist was a popular art movement in the early part of the 14th century. Connected vaguely to the reactionary movement at the time, it was steeped in mannered echos of tradition, religious imagery, and ancient cultural symbols. Symbolist art largely took the form of heroic paintings, depictions of religious visitations, and indefinitely featured figures looming in bewildering landscapes. Notable artists were Owun Sha-Tangpt, Vakt Aptazh, and Gozolobba Ninkazh.

Symbolist was a popular art movement in the early part of the 14th century. Connected vaguely to the reactionary movement at the time, it was steeped in mannered echos of tradition, religious imagery, and ancient cultural symbols. Symbolist music typically featured cryptic weedling melodies, and achaic revivals of bygone music. Important composers included Shan Sha-Shab, and Gazzamak Mazfag.

The praxiatical movement was largely inspired by functionalist pragmatics and antietiological notions of acausal phenomena. Determined to create unrepresentational and/or meaningless art, the praxiatical movement was, for some years, the enfant terrible of Ishahfazhi art circles. Praxiatical literature attempted to distill an pragmatic essence in literature, and often consisted of alltogether strange texts: unreadable screeds of sounds, oblique and paradoxical, recursive discourses, and tedious, mindless, repetitive novels. Important authors included Shanprak Sha-Gorod, Rau Ben-Tzymon, and Hrid Tzau-Aeum.

The praxiatical movement was largely inspired by functionalist pragmatics and antietiological notions of acausal phenomena. Determined to create unrepresentational and/or meaningless art, the praxiatical movement was, for some years, the enfant terrible of Ishahfazhi art circles. Praxiatical art attempted to distill a sense of colour-as-colour, texture-as-texture, and material-as-object, to disabuse the view of all possible representation notions. This involved both producting highly abstract shapes, as well the typically 'representative' works recontextualised by subtle differences in textures and perspectives. Important artists were Mrid Sha-Vaun, Gomalobba Kafazh, and Guth Kyush-so.

The praxiatical movement was largely inspired by functionalist pragmatics and antietiological notions of acausal phenomena. Determined to create unrepresentational and/or meaningless art, the praxiatical movement was, for some years, the enfant terrible of Ishahfazhi art circles. Praxiatical music attempted to distill an essence of pure, affective sound to overwhelm and reach immediately the passive listener. It consisted mostly of cacaphonics, as well as concordant discordance, and early forays into a-tonal music. Important composers included the great 'de-tuner' Oswid Sha-Mak.

The Modernist movement was chacterised by commitments to forms guided by use and function, absolutist political attitudes, and a clarification of the principles of praxiaticism. Rather than wanton indulgence in the shocking, the purely pragmatic or praxiatic, the modernist movement attempt to employ functionalist thinking to clarify tradional structures or depiction, representation, and living, leading to an emphasis on purity and abstraction, not a clumsy attempt toward the abstract itself. Modernist art featured thus non-natural colours, aperspectival presentations, and emphasis on shapes and orientations. Notable artists were Kungwu Sha-Tont, Gozbaja Bazzamak, and Thrakunt Betz-On.

The Modernist movement was chacterised by commitments to forms guided by use and function, absolutist political attitudes, and a clarification of the principles of praxiaticism. Rather than wanton indulgence in the shocking, the purely pragmatic or praxiatic, the modernist movement attempt to employ functionalist thinking to clarify tradional structures or depiction, representation, and living, leading to an emphasis on purity and abstraction, not a clumsy attempt toward the abstract itself. Modernist music featured a dramatic synthesis of traditional tunings, re-tunings, tonal music and atonal music. Important composers included Gyuthu Gog-so, Vophton Ghunngvheb, and Mungt Sha-Man.

The rise of a popular imperial culture dramatically changed the consumption and production of art. A broadly literate public, with wealth to read, consume, and be entertained, as well as fiercly patriotic and defensive of imperial wealth, contributed to the formation of what became known as the 'imperial style'. Pleasing, patriotic, sentimental, the cloying 'academic' style of painting and sculpture featured accessible representations of national triumphs, simplified ancient history, and military heroism, which was deeply loved by the wealthy and middle class of empire.

The rise of a popular imperial culture dramatically changed the consumption and production of art. A broadly literate public, with wealth to read, consume, and be entertained, as well as fiercly patriotic and defensive of imperial wealth, contributed to the formation of what became known as the 'imperial style'. Imperial style music often took the form of a jolly synthesis of military marches, and the folk music of the imperial periphary, and was typically played in taverns, plebian amphitheaters, racecources, and other areas of excitable recreation.

The rise of a popular imperial culture dramatically changed the consumption and production of art. A broadly literate public, with wealth to read, consume, and be entertained, as well as fiercly patriotic and defensive of imperial wealth, contributed to the formation of what became known as the 'imperial style'. A pulp literature of imperial triumps, colonial adventure stories, and lurid tales about the barbarous enemies of the state became popular among the middle classes especially.

The essentialist notion of asietic willing of being, described by Jêjor Yoguthâhu, birthed a curious art movement at the hight of the imperial epoch. Concluding that works of art, like all things, must will themselves into existence, groups of artists organised themselves around attempting to faciliate 'art creating itself' which involved several systems designed to allow art to create itself, by placing canvases in public places, developing complex systems of wind chimes, etc.

The wealth of the world, plundered from Kovazh, Bafozh, and the smaller continents faciliated truly a grand and quixotic wave of monument building in the late 14th century. The colossal spherical mausoleum for the desceased Vopudwou Praakungwu IX (r. 1353-1382) and the New Imperial Palace in Vokonazh are typical examples of this - towering above the surrounding countryside, requiring hundreds of thousands of tons of steel and concrete, these archiectural marvels are testament to the power and wealth that belonged to great imperial regimes of this time.

The large scale settlement of Ishahfazhis in parts of both Bafozh and Kovazh led to a fascination with 'colonial' and 'native' forms of art, both in 'popular' and 'high' cultures. Primitivim in art was well regarded by a certain sort of anthropologically minded elite in the metropole, as well as became the kitchsy trappings of colonial settlements.

Trancending the 'high modernist' style of earlier absolutist architecture, later absolutist styles fused imperial grandure with the form-functionalism of the earlier modernist movement, leading to an impressively grand brutalist synthesis. Particularly excellent examples of this sort of style are the Pan-Nâgine Congress Hall, and the Nozho Civil Directorate Building.

The Modernist movement was chacterised by commitments to forms guided by use and function, absolutist political attitudes, and a clarification of the principles of praxiaticism. Rather than wanton indulgence in the shocking, the purely pragmatic or praxiatic, the modernist movement attempt to employ functionalist thinking to clarify tradional structures or depiction, representation, and living, leading to an emphasis on purity and abstraction, not a clumsy attempt toward the abstract itself. Modernist literature was decidedly stilted and formal, a sort of academic style veiled in notions of revealing pragmatic expressions in tradional forms. Deeply mannered, it was typically the purview of statist bureaucrats and the Poumnian elite, who maintained their unique ability to maintain a 'high' culture in an increasingly demotic age.

Shov Sha-Rushman was the first one to effectively mathematise economic speculation, developing a number of proposed relationships between variables. As a leading figure in the 'third wave' of economic speculation, he would be a key figure in economic orthodoxy.

Dhofmazhi Zhakd was a major correspondent with Shov Sha-Rushman, and a major newspaper man in Gaubja. He was a major populariser of Rushmanian economic thought, as well as a member of the Gaubjan economic reform league.

Hwamp Puur was a major critic of the quickly established orthodoxy of Sha-Rushman's thought. He challenged the notion that economics was representable by a priori methods such as mathematics, and commited himself to a descriptivist and empiricist account of economics.

Dhomak Mâzfa was the first thinker to seriously apply the functionalist philosophy to economic thought, which gave birth to the 'operationist' school of economics. Trade, to some extent, as it did very little beyond move things around, became nearly immaterial to what consisted of 'the economy'. Mâzhfa priortised studying factors of production.

Mobauk Mizava was a desciple of Dhomak Mâzfa. He extended Mâzfa's analysis of 'pure growth' to a larger 'thermodynamic' energic system, where he declared the only fit subject of economics was the study of the sun, solar energy, and other heaveny things which appear to produce their own energy.

Bâzajopt Kushkt was the first statist theorist of economics. He suggest that the state take control of all factors of production to ensure proper management, and reduce 'unreal' phenomena like trade distorition created by speculators and retailers.

Dimash Kushkt was the brother of the more famous Bâzajopt Kushkt, and a close desciple of his. He studied living conditions in industrial slums in Bagh, and provided his brother with the data that he would use to argue that state control of factors of production would reduce both the suffering of the common man and increase efficiency.

Bida Fovkazh was a factory manager in Jiishanâg who quickly adopted functionalist-statist principles in his operation. By refusing to sell a large number of his goods and rendering them directly to his workers, and attempting to set up an autarkic system, he was a pioneer of the statist cartel firms that would so trouble governments in the early 14th century.

Yomeg Og Yezoz was a Takemogine longshoreman who worked in the dockywards in Seikaukz. Exposed to functionalist and statist critiques, he attempted to agitate both the government and his employers to do more for the working industrial classes. He would later join the parliament as the first electee of the Takemogi statist party.

Makoun Sha-Gosod Sha-Man, a scion of the illustrious Poumnian aristocratic house of Sha-Gosod Sha-Man, which would also produce the later, better known Vufo Sha-Gosod Sha-Man, agitated by what he described as 'demotic' and 'sickeningly plebian gashdzoun thinking' economic thought, especially statism, described an economic system where he believed that there were naturally aristocratic classes in every society and economic, and natural slave peoples, and there was no point in reforming the economy.

Droum Sha-Mushim was an economist of the school of what would come to be called the 'organical school'. The organical school emphasised the historical and cultural development of economic systems, drawing on the work of Hwamp Puur.

Jêbun Yannagath was an organicist economist from the Rannu Empire. He criticised the industrial developement in society and was a major interpreter of Tehuhrite law in context of modern economic developments.

Foda Nagjoni was a numismatician, who complied a large catalogue of the history of coinage in Ishahfazh. His work incidentally contained a number of monetary theories, grounded in organicist thinking.

Shrumu Mruuwun was another major member of the organistic school. Long a professor in the Studium of Prousorum, his works on value largely gradually descended into apologetics for the Poumnian regime.
Druut Sha-Mang was a major theorist of war economy, and public financing. He studied historical methods of loan raising by governments, and became an early theoretician of trust.
Nokodopau Vokuma was a Vokonazhi aristocrat and planter, who became an early agronomist, as well as a reactionary advocate, describing a paternalistic and pastoralist 'folk economy'.

Vufo Sha-Gosod Sha-Man was a highly influential economist, who may be said to be the 'economist of empire'. Suggesting that large, self suficient economic blogs can run up colossal debts to finance imperial wars, he justified the arms race of the late 14th century by appeal to high government debt spending as a drive of demand and economic growth.
Guabjim Fauzhkt was the first finance minister of the Nâgine absolutist government. He advocated for large scale printing of money to finance the various nagine war efforts.

Buro Tugot-So was a major member of the Athisoroon parliament's 'tarrif party'. He advocated repeatedly raising tarrifs, and borrowing and spending extensively, in accordance with the Gosodian school.

Masogu Foma-So was one of the few dissenting voices in the heydey of Godosian economics. By clining to a liberationist economy, grounded in organically acting small producers, and echewing debt, he was a relict of the organicist school.
Fimpo Sha-Pomp was one of the few poumnian adopters of operationalism. He was a major student of production efficency and economy of scale.

The instituional school was one of the most developed economic schools of the 14th century. It was centered around the person and work of Dhomâmak Maptazh, who argued that instituions, customs, and states shape markets, as well as market behaviour. His rationalistic method allowed for a great degree of study of many topics within an institutionalist paradigm.

Mazupt Pazhkash was a major student of marginality. He came to this in fact in terms of studying 'losses' incurred in taxation, by the tax payer, in his studies of the effects of taxation on market behaviour.
Boddamag Gidazh was an important student of social behaviour and consumption. His studies bled into sociology. He was a professor at the studium of Nozho.

Wroushou Tzamutzi was one of the first complete student of markets: how they come into being, the different sorts of markets (e.g. thin vs thick) and how markets take on definite characters related to trust and regulation.
Kib Mroud was a Poumnian exponent of the instituional school. He drew on the work of the precursors of the instituional school, especially his countryman Voun Sha-Pomid.
Zadak Optazh was an instituionalist student of household economics. He studied the reasons everyday persons make economic choices.

Mahdmaut Maktazh was an instituionalist student of the role of technological development in economic growth: the role of research in accounting for gaps in traditional economic theory's explanation of the astounding growth that came with industrialisation.
Pruudum Sha-Trunguntwu was a theorist of economic epistemology: how the economic of information effects economic choices and behaviour.

Orumuu Vorid was a theorist of land usage. Particularly, he connected theories of marginality to land usage, and suggested reasons for colonial expansions were a consequence of increasingly poor returns on occupying new land in a given land market.
Middanak Doshkva was a theorist of the sociology of business enterprises and their role in shaping consumption patterns. He studied avaliability and substituion.
Pâazahpt Dazhpt was a theorist of market cycles. He attempted to understand why crashes happened, and came to the conclusion that they were driven by excessive production.
Nobamedes Zhakdi was a theorist of market cycles. He attempted to understand why crashes happened, and came to the conclusion that they were driven by limits to the money supply.
Mraakunt Sha-Mong was a theorist of historical technological growth. He suggested that thin markets were vulnerable to knowledge loss.

The liberationist impulse began to falter slowly after the achievement of the Worldly liberationist state after the shattering of the Athisard monarchy. Failing ultimately to deliver the promised paradise, the liberationist state quickly became a tyranny in its own right. Clumsy, violent, and despotic, the dictacts from the central government failed to perfectly reflect and paternally guide the popular will. Amid speculation on improvement and reform, parallel to the growth of the statist ideology, briefly flourished the thought of the truly impressive Soora Egat-so. This radical pamphleteer, preacher, militant, and philosopher took the Liberationist ideology to a radical extreme: rather than a divine polity guided by the gods, and sanctioned by the will of man, Egat called for the repudiation of all political authority beyond the treaty between two sovereign individuals. In a collection of pamphlets known as the “Mystic Secrets” series (1316-7), Egat builds a cosmology based on the willing soul and the certainty of a world beyond, from which he develops an admirable contractualist political philosophy. Egat was killed in the hills near Sesi by forces of the Sublime Veyethan government defending a radical commune who repudiated the government’s authority.

The principles of liberationist philosophy and government emphasize the cooperative enterprise, particularly the maintenance of the commons and the streets. Everyone had a responsibility to scare the birds, to cobble the streets, and small guilds and assemblies were usually used to maintain these institutions, rather than give way to the relentless pressure of industrial expansion. In the years of liberationist experimentation, there was the practical result of the arrival of a number of cooperativist dogmatists, who preached cooperativism as a basic political given and good, whether in the fields, the factory, the government, or the army. The views, ideas and actions of these syndics, guildists, cooperativsts are most exemplified in Rajug Duttûnnony’s “Study of the Organisation of Manufactuaries in the Southern Empire” (1320). The syndicate would become a critical institution in Absolutist theory of government.

A very popular political cause and much dogmatised position in the early fourteenth century was that of the Antidevelopmentalist. Hating the advent of the machines that came to remark the world and the countryside, that drove down wages, created great slums, and made the cruel burgher even richer, many of various political and social inclinations came to be sure of the need to chain the wheels of industry. In a popular melody, the “Bahdro Blower’s Lament”, the narrator tells of the tragic lives of the Bahdro glass blowers, who used to make much of the loamy, sandy soil and the need for the bottling of the Magoupt oils, but now cannot find a job due to glass produced in the furnaces of Rodhrot.

Born out of dint of necessity in managing a modern industrial civilisation and Statist speculation, the 1320s and 30s were filled with innovations for the management of people and societies, as well as innovations in the way states managed themselves. Particularly, in the school of disciplinary thought, traditional floggings, whippings, oubliettes, and hangings moved to a broader system of indefinite detentions, implicit blackmail, disappearances, and conspicuous yet sparse violence. An outgrowth of the authoritarian impulse, much of the innovation in this field came in the rationalization of these methods, and the application of them not only to the troublesome populace, but also the appendages of the state itself. The practical system of disciplinary reform by inspector Drid Tzau-Thruunt was highly influential. In his tenure of office as the Mreuvayk prefecture district inspector, 1324-9, he developed a broadly systematic approach to internal discipline the gendarmerie that prioritized an integrated system of incentives, cultivated collective identity, and humiliating punishments that bound officers to the state, and allowed for the easy social exclusion and then removal of troublesome men.

The staggering pluralism of the modern world emerged as a challenge for the modern government. Atheists, secularists, sectarian zealots, mystics, practitioners of foreign cults, and the great masses of heathen believers in the imperialised periphery presented a great babble of disagreement, and were easily stirred to conflict and hatred of one government or the other. A rationalized system of approved cults and faiths, and the vigorous suppression of those deemed socially unhygienic, based explicitly on expectation of social coherency and public order, broadly emerged as the states of Ishahfazh grappled both with unorthodox at home and heathen subjects in the colonies. In the early stations and factories established by the Gaubjan government in the Juuruntine territories, we learn directly of the various permits and writs needed for traditional J’ur meeting places to be maintained, and there a few interesting records of the various considerations Gaubjan bureaucrats enquired and worried about during these hearings.

Gozomedes' Great Game (GGG) is a Victoria II mod set in a fictional world populated by alternate hominids, largely based on the Australopithecus. The world of GGG (the Miiv) lies on a planetary sphere that is roughly the same size as earth, and spins also with a tilted axis. It is dominated by three major continents: Ishahfazh, Kovazh, and Bafozh, which are accompanied by three sub-continental shelves: Paukzhodo, Shobgizob, and Gofakidzia. The world itself is a watery world, dominated by vast and deep oceans, and the major continents lie close together, lining the few easily navigable seas. Beyond this area of calm, the vast oceanic geography cultivates the development of massive, nigh continuous storms, especially in the vast empty ocean of the north of the planet.\nThe concurrent presence of multiple intelligent and significantly genetically different species has led to a number of notable differences between the world of GGG and our own. Above all, the world lacks any sort of enlightenment universalism, and people persist in a number of practices that would seem savage in our own world, above all the keeping of other hominids as ‘thralls’ or cattle-slaves for eating and working. Beyond this, transcultural hostility remains higher, the world is largely more violent, and diplomatic practices bereft of any notions of international law, balances of power, common heritage, etc. There are a variety of notable species: Ishahfazh is mainly populated by the stout and hairy folk who make up most of the large empires (Gashdzii, Poumnian, Sithevan), but the Byotrin (Ghech, Anuvo, Shagmodt) people are tall, hairless, flat faced, white skinned giants living the central regions, and the Oujoy and Unnahu are large eyed and thin. The peoples of the east and centre of Kovazh (the Qooxib, Ourrhond) are decidedly smaller, and have features more similar to those of the capuchin or macaque monkeys of our world. In the wilds of Bafozh one finds strange beast men, hominidae with blue faces, and all sorts in between.

In southern Ishahfazh has risen a dynamic, now industrial collection of civilisations, the foremost among these being the Old Gashdzii Empire and its successor states, the ancient theocratic Poumnian Empire, and the fractious Sithevan peoples of the west around the state of Athis or Veyethu. It is worth surveying the history of these civilisations. Poumnia, through its various dynasties and dynastic cycles, is ruled by the eternal Pudwou, the supposed God-Emperor and his noble retainers and governors. It has remained for the past millennia a relatively cohesive state. It lies in the Poudwouvas river delta ecosystem in the southern lands of Ishahfazh, notable for growing the euphoria inducing Pruub flower and the rivergrain that has fed the Poumnian civilization. Most of the people of Poumnia live on the rivers, cultivating grain and living in mud or stilt houses. The Poumnian civilisation is part of a larger continuum of the Diwvish languages and peoples, who also include the seafaring rugged Pruunts of the southern peninsula, and the jungle dwelling Roshupt and Towuzhians, most of whom remain nominal or actual vassals of the Poumnian empire to this day. Out of wars and political conflicts in Poumnian antiquity, which was fraught with many warring noble houses all claiming some degree of divinity or divine tutelage emerged the Vopudwou, or the Pudwou, the divine emperor, who subdued and pacified other nobles, extending his divine grace to these ‘lesser deities’. The Poumnian state developed a proud military, and a highly authoritarian, stratified tradition of governance, for many years maintaining a powerful grasp on its own lands and its environs.

The Gashdzii empire emerged around 1200 years ago, out of a small number of plateau dwelling folk in the central savannah of Ishahfazh. At this time much of the Savannah was inhabited by the ancestors of the Byotrin, peoples speaking relatives of Proto-Gashdziik, and peoples speaking now-dead languages perhaps related to the Pagyuti of the southern peninsula. The massive Gashdzii empire, founded by Godhiinimiz I (r. 102-149 i.r.) became a force for the settlement, colonisation, and assimilation of massive swathes of central Ishahfazh, only running up against the might of the Poumnians in the south, and inhospitable deserts and dense jungles in the north and east respectively. The majority of the Gashdzii practice Kadkohi, the idolatrous faith lauding the four high spirits that rule the world. For nearly 800 years the empire centred around Pashdzii, the Imperial city, remained powerful and influential, until a number of political and economic circumstances precipitated the slow disentanglement of the empire. The imperial successor states continued to pay lip service to the empire, but began engaging increasingly in their own endeavours. Particularly on the southern coasts, the Jiishanagi and the Gaubjans, along with a reinvigorated Poumnia, engaged in the exploration and exploitation of the southern and eastern continents, settling, colonising, warring and trading, eventually shifting the apex of the world market to the circle sea on which lies Nozho of Jiishanag and the many ports of the Poumnians.

A gradual concentration of markets and wealth facilitated increasing scientific and engineering knowledge as merchants scrambled to create weaponry and textiles to export to the hinter and hither continents. Burgeoning populations, more powerful weaponry, and more taxes as a result of flourishing trade and industry facilitated the creation of more centralised states. Gradually, an industrial and modern society was emerging on the southern shores of the circle sea. Meanwhile, the old lands of the Gashdzii empire experienced dramatic political and religious changes. The old iron grip of the deity-focused synods was challenged by the anti-magisterial movement, which challenged clerical authority. The preachings of Kauzhut ‘Mifachâzhafta’ ‘the great diviner’, and Kauzhut ‘Donavvat’ ‘the describer’ founded the jurico-ethical heretical Motkhonic faith which spread across the south. The anti-magisterial movement precipitated a large-scale series of uprisings and instability, crystallizing into the ‘liberationist’ movement which came to challenge not only clerical but also aristocratic power. As we come to the modern age, the ancient Sithevan monarchy of the house of Athis was shattered by the revolutionary liberationist movement of the Sublime Veyethu, now the foremost revolutionary state. The Poumnians must grapple with consolidating regional power in a changing world, and the various Gashdzii look to reconstruct the old empire or develop new and modern political configurations. In the far reaches of the north, the Sedentarian, or Tehuhrite monarchies, always lagging a bit behind the south, must be gradually awakening and modernising.\n\nAt game start, the international political sphere remains dynamic and unstable: lands are opening up for colonization, political leaders seek to restore fallen empires, and ancient kingdoms seek to keep a stranglehold on power.

On the great plains of the continent of Ishahfazh, by the imperial reckoning, the year is 1308. For the past four hundred years, since the traumatic and prolonged shattering of the Gashdzii empire in the times of sorrow, the face of Ishahfazh has been transformed by a series of events and innovations, the implications of which are only now becoming clear. A steady trickle of exploration has mapped the world and brought more and more regions into a global market, while vicious competition, politically and economically, has driven the proliferation of new forms of economic organization and innovations. At the same time, Gashdzii society has been wracked by perennial social upheaval since the collapse of the empire. The traditional lordly and ecclesiastical domination has been steadily challenged in more unstable regions, leading to the gradual development of what has been termed the "social liberationist" movement, rejecting centralized ecclesiastical organization. This movement, already tinged with social radicalism, in recent years has taken a critically radical turn. Calling themselves "liberationists" or "free-yokers", these radicals seek to overthrow the traditional organization of society at large. Calling for the abolition of proprietary social rights, manorial society, and aristocratic privilege, they seek to establish a society that caters to the common people, and to a traditional agricultural and arcadian lifestyle. As the game begins, the states of Ishahfazh are set poised for a vast confrontation as the very fabric of society changes: the merchants and industrials of the south look to command the very planet by their clever technologies, while the social liberationists across the former empire and its peripheries look to the Sitheve liberationist state with all their hopes for a worldly paradise, and in the ancient Poumnian empire and the great Vokonazh domains of the North, the forces of reaction and aristocracy rally their armies...

The recent successful military action by reactionary cadres has caused the total overthrow of our nation’s government. Revolutionary guards organized by radicalized noblemen and clerical dissenters seized the major arteries of government in $CAPITAL$, causing most of the remaining legitimate government to flee or resign. The capital remains in a somber mood after the closure of frantic violence in the streets. Citing causes of tradition, legitimacy, the ancestral faith, and the divinely ordained order, they have rolled back political and social privileges dramatically. The parliament has been suspended, and rapidly a number of edicts restoring the old nobility and church to positions have been promulgated. This will be sure to cause domestic unrest, as well as has destabilized our position abroad as local governments attempt to regularize relations with the new regime. It remains to be seen how this will affect the development of our country long term.
Reaction is the order of the day, it seems.

The recent successful seizure of power by the theocratist paramilitary faction in $CAPITAL$ has affected a radical transformation of our state. After the brutal capture of the city, the theocratists forced a mass resignation of most officials, and performed a couple of particularly brutal religious killings of a number of non-compliant social activists and former governmental elites. They have rapidly set up a parallel bureaucracy as an outgrowth of their paramilitary faction’s political secretariat, and have quickly and violently enforced Theocratic control over much of the rest of the country though local gauleiter and collaborating clergy. Ultimately state power now rests in theory within the national theocratist synod, the collection of life-term clerics and internally elected party functionaries that head the political and military direction of the theocratist party.
I’ll see you at worship, then, fonctionnaire…

The recent seizure of $CAPITAL$ by radical bands of 'Free-Yokers' has dramatically transformed the political constitution of our country. In their iconoclastic crusade against all symbols of privilege, aristocracy, and clericalism, they have routed the last government supporters that continued to fight and hung those which they could capture. Proclaiming the rights of the citizen-farmer and the “unfettered national spirit”, they have established a radical directorate committee to direct the “preservation of the national corps”, which has assumed most governmental powers for the time being. The central government in the meantime has passed a number of radical edicts, guaranteeing the privileges of the yeoman farmer as well as the rural laborer and the urban menu peuple, establishing labor regulation boards, grain distribution laws, encouraging anti-competitive and protective economic policies, and abolishing aristocratic privilege.
Hurrah for the popular will, I say!

The recent capture of our seat of government by the so-called $COUNTRY_ADJ$ Absolutist Army Faction has ushered in an age of new and shockingly different governments. Proclaiming the ‘age of the state’ begun, in the central square of $CAPITAL$, now rechristened ‘State Square’, the reconstruction of society began with the total abolition of identities beyond ‘citizen’, and it is clear that paramount leadership seems to lie in the bureaucratic secretariat or the military-political commissariate. Most state offices have either been awarded by appointment by the party leadership, or have been abolished and reshaped. Much private land has been seized as “wastage” for alternative usage, and a number of “inefficiencies, abuses, and crimes” have been abolished. It seems that in the foreseeable future our country will be under the strict and punctual leadership of a swarm of party functionaries, teachers, shop-floor managers and agricultural overseers.
Why, good chap, I believe that’s quorum!

Recently, a certain group of new political theorists in $COUNTRY$, stimulated, they say, by a reflection upon the perennial disorders of war, industrial recession, famine, inefficiency, have diagnosed the source of society's ills as not one of inequality or political radicalism, but one of 'anarchy'. Growing out of social liberationist speculation, they have arrived at the conclusion that despite the correct impulses of liberationism, the current state cannot correctly support its intentions. Claiming the current state is ill suited to deal with modern material civilization - the various industrial innovations that have reshaped the economic and attendant social order of the day - they propose a radical reorganization of the state along the lines of the most efficient industrial and corporate enterprises. Endorsing all reforms to rid the state of inefficiency, by means centralized planning, a needed expression of state bureaucracy, rationalization of legislation, elimination of autonomy, etc, the 'statist' ideology demands that the state itself be rationalized to save the gains of social libertarianism from the new ills of inefficiency and the vagaries of the market.

Ever since the increased agitation of statist reforms and political organization, a new, more virulent and extreme form of statism has emerged from a circle of intellectuals in $COUNTRY$ out of frustration with the statist impulse to compromise with and even protect Liberationist reforms. Turning their back on statism's roots as a means for the preservation of social Liberationism, they have come to suggest that the state itself is an 'absolute' good, an entity that serves no greater good than itself. They cry that the efficiency and capacity of the state must be enforced and pursued 'absolutely', with total indifference to petty squabbling and selfish demands of its constituents. This, they claim, will ultimately, and exclusively, bring true prosperity to those members of the state, unlike the illusions of other ideologies which bring only selfish gain to certain members of the state. Ultimately the absolutist impulse is a radical reformulation and indeed clarification of the purpose and even very being of the state: the state should be seen as an enterprise that succeeds or fails in the preservation and expansion of its own power, capacity, and efficiency, and nothing else.

The principles of conservatism and reaction have long languished in the doldrums of opposition and desperate compromise. Now, however, we are seeing the revival of the forces of reaction. The 'theocratist' speculators of $COUNTRY$ make radical claims: everywhere, fat and useless bureaucracies deliver grains to idle vagrants and wastrels who have been uprooted from their ancestral homes, great slum tenements have risen up in our once bright cities, the humble farmer is ruined by the slump in the prices of commodities, and mankind wallows, spiritually blighted by this atheistic age of worldly delights. And so a voice hearkens for the halcyon days of yore, when each man knew his station and worked the land of a fatherly lord. A day when each man did not indulge in strange, synthetic compounds, or interpret scriptures in his own degenerate way, but listened to the strictures of the educated priest. But how to achieve this, in such an age of markets and factories? The theocratist ideology claims that the authoritarian and centralizing implements of the modern state pioneered by statism must be employed in fact explicitly for the sake of moral edification and social order.

Conscripts are being drafted left and right and the poor are being trained and prepared to fight. Military camps are full of fresh recruits, troops are carrying out exercises in our borders and every aspect of society and every signal the government gives seems to indicate a war is in progress, yet there's no war. This large disruption in the country's daily life is angering our population and making our neighbours increasingly wary.

Recent reforms in our state have dramatically elevated the significance and constitutional role of a number of religious authorities and bodies. This preponderant influence of the clergy and faith institutions in decision making, legislation, and judgment means our state most properly ought to be described as a 'theocracy' above anything else. Gradually, through the influence of the courts and religious police, much of the nominally “secular” government has become beholden to religious authorities, and has melded into one structure. Religious discourse dominates the public sphere, and there is at this point very few who would not publicly profess the state faith.

Recent reforms in our country have graduated centralized power around a single authoritarian personage of an aristocratic dynasty, suggesting that at this point it is probably appropriate to call our country a “princely despotate”, as per the common parlance. This creeping shift has occurred as the executive has gradually gained power by the slow removal of special ecclesiastical dominion, as well as centralized the bureaucracy in the hands of loyalist bourgeois officeholders. The effective decline of aristocratic power in active governance has weakened the parliament with the rise of the power of the prince. Local magnates and squires in the countryside are bewailing a decline in “natural liberties” and “the old constitution and our beloved commonwealth”, and clerics are warning of a “new secularism”, but it seems most subjects have quiescently accepted the augmented power of our monarch, who increasingly formalizes their power by the day, as the royal court grows more sure of itself.
Well, at least it will cut down on squabbling...

Our state has recently undergone a number of critical political changes related to political decentralization, corporate legislation, and aristocratic privilege, such that we might at this point call our country an “aristocratic commonwealth”. Power lies now first and foremost amongst a body of great noble proprietors collaborating in a parliamentary body. The gradual devolution of both the regional executive and judicial powers to local aristocratic magnates has enabled the graduate capture of the country by these great barons and marcher lords. While this generally bodes poorly for the serf and whatever remnants of an executive remain, most burghers and yeomen have silently accepted the changes, integrating themselves into the increasingly aristocratic structures through town charters and elective corporations. It is not long, surely, before the executive is nigh more than a figurehead, and the church is all but private property of the local lord, some are saying.
Two, or six hundred, heads, are better than one?

The practice of serfdom - land-labour bondage of all types, has been abolished in all manners in our nation. All banalities, corvee, tributes, and levies have been strictly banned. This is likely to enrage many great aristocrats and their servants, who hate to see this ancient rite disappear. They bewail the end of the bond between lord and villein, an ancient bond going far back into yore. However, these dues have long worn upon our people, and the rural folk resent greatly these impositions on their lives. Many considered these restrictions on movement, land usage, and labor sales a great drag on our economy as well. The so-called 'serf problem', which has created many dilapidated estates and rural slums, will hopefully be gradually cleared up by this effort to suppress these unjust dues, regularize our economy and land usage, and make these families a functioning part of our markets.
Well, that will make these folk jolly!

The barbaric practice of thralldom - the rearing, culling, vending, driving, transhumance, pasturing, breeding, and above all consuming the flesh of hominid cattle, or ‘thralls’ has finally been abolished in our country. This will greatly enrage all traditionalists of various types - great landowners, wretched yeomen, and consumers with a certain taste for man flesh. Nonetheless, its quite clear that this clumsy and strange practise was a great drag on our economy and our moral decency as a state. Now these able bodies folk will surely be free to join the economy, and we will no longer have the stain of near-cannibalism on our consciousness.

A fortification is something tricky to maintain - not only it needs regular assessment of the integrity of walls and gates, but also a constant supply of new armaments, supplies and tools for repair. If one of these ingredients are missing, the structures become useless and the military corps are powerless to stop decay from setting in. After several years of hardship, what is seen in $STATENAME$ is this picture, a consequence of the disastrous bankruptcy that is crushing $COUNTRY$.

Our civilisation is a truly ancient one - for millennia our people have worked on the vast paddies and swamplands that constitute the great Poudwouvas river valley. Thousands of years of careful earthworks, dredging, canal construction, and bank reinforcement have turned our great, vast river and its mangroves into carefully cultivated fertile paddies for the harvest of riverseed and Pruub flower. Huge mud and root embankments of dense, drooping mangroves line the cuts and gullies to protect from excessive flooding, and provide channels for the barges and gondolas to gently pass through. The houses of our people lie on elegant stilts, or their mud dwellings rest safely atop vast stones moved centuries ago in forgotten engineering feats. When his majesty the Vopudwou, the celestial emperor, the very lynchpin of the world, looks upon his vast domain in the morning, when the rays of the sun kiss the paddies, he can be sure that his civilisation will be bountiful and enduring for the unending future.

An adventurous sort of man, an ex-lieutenant, a self-styled explorer who’s spent time in the far east among the locals, who came into a private fortune by either smuggling, trading, or inheritance (the matter remains murky), has seemingly drummed up a lot of enthusiasm about leading a small band of reservists, thugs, and other martial men to take over some godforsaken chiefdom or other in the wild beyond, with which he seems to be somehow sordidly personally entangled, due to his travels. Most pertinently, he’s passed a request to the foreign secretary actually asking for ships and means to achieve this, promising to incorporate these lands into our state.

About fourteen months ago, our foreign office and exchequer, for better or for worse, provided a soldier of fortune with means to make himself master of a small undeveloped region beyond our shores. His unkempt soldiers shuffled into their vessels in an unspectacular way, and with little fanfare left our wharfs for distant shores, to scant notice outside of certain circles. Staggeringly, however, we have just received a formal communique from this man who informs us that he and his men have mastered this distant land, and established a small colonial government. He wishes to hand over a government of ‘protectorate’ to the colonial office, in exchange only for a number of handsome concessions on commercial prospects and trading regions, and large parcels of land for himself and his soldiers, as well as a small lifelong stipend from the state. It’s better to have such an ambitious man overseas, anyhow, says the minister of the interior.

It has now been over fourteen months since we last heard from this adventurer. Rumor has it that he and his men were eaten alive by beast-men in Shobgizob, or vanquished in battle in some cursed desert in Bafozh, or simply destroyed by a great ocean storm before they had even stepped foot on foreign lands. Regardless, it is safe to assume that this adventurer and his men are long dead, our money wasted, and our officials made to look foolish for ever trusting this soldier of fortune.
Never again will I trust another fool with an expensive dream!

About fourteen months ago, someone, surely sacked now, in the government made the dubious call to provide a roguish and dashing fellow with the substantial means to master a small overseas region for our own colonial aggrandizement. Now, however, we are receiving reports that while this chap did manage to make himself master of this region, he has been decidedly silent in communicating with our government, and is actually styling himself as a local king after intermarrying with local nobility! Him and his thugs have made themselves the effective elites of the region, and have even had the gall to begin encouraging settlements from our mainland! While he has managed to extend the norms of our government across the region, all in all it is a huge embarrassment for the foreign office to have this little tyrant renege on his promises to hand over governance and to continue to live as a prince on our dime!
This blackguard and his rogue state must be brought to justice!

The colonial frontier is always a flexible thing - indeed, all frontiers and borderlands are. Porous and shifting, these regions admit the passage of settlers, traders, laborers, ranchers, trappers, and the border itself encourages the mercenary trade, the suttler’s trade, and the development of mixed frontier communities. However, sometimes these territories can ignite into great conflagrations of tension. This is what happened recently at one of our colonial borders - it’s not exactly clear what has happened, but it appears some movement of settlers has provoked a raid of a sort that ended in massacre. Local gazetteers are crying out for blood, and settler violence has already flared up in an alarming way. The local colonial governor is actually recommending sending soldiers to take over and pacify the bordering region to prevent excesses, establish a new secure frontier, and address all regional security concerns.
Their lands will fall under our banner!
This is simply not possible at this moment
