English: In one of our provinces there is a new political movement that has organised itself. Under one particularly active man, apparently an artisan who has been driven out of business by the new machines, there is a league agitating for the curtailment of capital and technological industry. They have formed into small gangs, smashing machines, singing songs denouncing capital, and have appealed to local aristocrats to maintain a ‘customs’ barrier, demanding the curtailment of local industry and the protection of the guilds via regulations. They have even, on occasion, made trouble for members of the constabulary and the gendarme who have been posted by regional authorities to protect factors, machinery, and other implements of industry. The issue has seemingly festered, and the league has become practically a militant reactionary group, attracting all sorts of troublemakers: aristocratic pretenders, conservative rabble, and mere opportunists.
Bah, I don't have time for this reactionary drivel
This dangerous seditionist and his followers must be put to death!

Our recent defeat by a great modern power has compelled us, as well as paying them extortionate sums of money, to establish a government that tolerates the various extraterritorial concessions we have made. Along with signing away a number of ports, they’ve wrung from us a great many railway concessions, and stipulated that the only political authority they will tolerate is that of the modernisers who respect these treaties. These wretched men have formed a government in $CAPITAL$, with the begrudging presence of our head of state, and the company of a number of smarmy representatives of the modern power, who were insufferably smug throughout the event.

The Diminutive State of Sog was organised by our forces, under famous general Mrakun Sha-Gosod, in his protracted invasion of what was still then partially Athisoron lands, after the Vewugist revolution of 1297. The war lasted nearly 7 years, and Sha-Gosod had maintained the Sog region as his base of operations in the war against the Veyethun, but, since no formal treaty was signed, even after the end of hostilities in 1305, we didn’t decamp from Sog until 1307. Sog has, since then, remained basically under the control of the same conservative collaborators. Now, however, since hostilities have broken out again with the Sithevans, the chief of staff has suggested we establish military governance over Sog for the sake of once again establishing a base of operations against the Siethevans. The problem is, Sog maintains nominal independence - the military seems in favour of issuing a perfunctory communique and simply crushing the Sogan government if they resist.

The Poumanian Foreign Ministry has issued a short communique declaring to us their intention to once again occupy Sog as a military protectorate, and to suspend our nominal diplomatic independence, as well as control of our borders!
Ancestral Home of the Midodazh Family

The county of Midod was first described in the early 300s, I.R., and by the mid 400s, in the reign of Godhiimâdho the fat, we find imperial records of regional office holders in the Vokonazh describing a castellan family ‘Midodazh’ [of Midod]. Dhov Gaumishig Midodazh was made lord of the Voshkt, a substantially greater territory, and from his serfs organised a powerful and effective army, with the lords of the Voshkt gradually assuming more and more power in the Vokonazh borderlands. In the struggle between Ishahmenes II of Vokonazh and Emperor Bozzamâdho IV, who reconquered the northern principalities, and disributed them among lesser men, Midod, in fact, was lost, but House Midodazh was already certain masters of the east. Now, Gozomedes II, heir to this great lineage, has reconquered Midod. Visiting his family sepulchres, and even the great cairns built by his oldest ancestors, his loyal soldiery tremble at this man of destiny who stands equal to the emperors of old.
May Gozomedes and his kin pray at the familial sepulchre once again!

The Holy Yauje Valley is the birthplace of the Sedentarian Faith. The ‘virtues of the solid man’ were first proclaimed by the Philosopher-King Osjunnet in this very valley, where he ruled the city state of Gohn-Peth, one of the oldest neolithic sites in Ishahfazh, around nearly 5000 years ago. This great lawgiver brought order to the restless nomads in the hinterlands beyond his borders, in the Sem flatlands. He taught how mother earth and father sky raise together harmonious life through agriculture, duty, and timeless order. But for many centuries, this holy land, where one can still see the old neolithic towers, was defiled and destroyed by another sort of nomad: the Bogoran Vewugist conquers, in the 6th century, in their brutality and wanton carelessness, drove many ancient sedentarian settlers from this old land. But now this ancient injustice is righted! Now we, a Tehuhrite people, finally rule this land again, and all rejoice for justice is done!
And we shall hold it for another changeless 5000 years.

The Pagans of $FROMCOUNTRY$ have long been a concern of major Vewugist missions. Long gone are the days when our force of arms were vastly superior to those of our neighbours, and Vewugism spread easily on the back of the conquest. Today we send missionaries around the world, to live amongst the pagans, spread religious catechisms, and evangelise the heathen, spreading the favour of the Vewug, and gaining his favour in doing so. One mission group in $FROMCOUNTRY$ has recently in fact reached out to us, communicating to us that they believe the local potentate there is close to conversion, and that some impressive gifts and some scholars, the means to establish a press publish texts, all to translate texts to their tongue and distribute them, would surely secure $FROMCOUNTRY$ to the patrimony of the great Vewug! The foreign office is the official guarantee for missionary societies, and must decide what to do.
They will have all that they need!
We can spare some of what they ask for
We have a few coins laying around the coffers, right?

The Red Flux is a truly sickening disease that causes unending bloody vomit and diarrhea, followed by hemorrhaging of blood from all orifices, and leaves survivors marred by small red pockmarks caused by inflammation of the skin. Called 'The Poumnian Gift', its belived that reservoirs of the pathogen lurk in the turgid and warm waters of the great Pudwouvas river, for this is where the disease most frequently strikes and then spreads from. Typically, the disease destroys its hosts so rapidly that it cannot spread quite far, but it seems like an alarmingly virulent strain of the red flux has emerged in one of our lands. It’s not exactly clear how it emerged, but the scenes of the hospitals in the region where it first emerged are truly gruesome, caked in blood and bodily refuse, with hopeless medics fleeing from patients who are left to die in pools of their own fluids. These are dark times, and religious authorities are declaring this a punishment of transmundane power, while individuals brace for what could be an alarming pandemic of the red flux!

The so-called ‘Wasting Sickness’ is an extremely ancient illness. Characterized by hair loss, atrophy, the breaking down of skin into large lesions, loosening of the skin from the bones, creating the ghastly appearance of a corpse in the victim, it has for millenia fuelled nightmares and terror of ghouls and the living dead, those afflicted are typically killed, shunned, and isolated. Experts speculate that it first emerged in Hominid populations with the rise of animal husbandry and agriculture, due to its spread by the vector of flies, who bite festering wounds and then spread this to the healthy tissue in others. The disease seemingly has been absent in many parts of the civilised world for quite some time, but it seems that this has changed. It seems that, somehow, the disease has found its way into fly populations again, and doctors are noting a terrifying rise in necrotising flesh in the population at large. Primitive measures of insect control, such as jars of sugary water, mitigate the spread somewhat, but those working in animal agriculture or in food handling in general are particularly at risk. It remains to be seen if this outbreak will get worse.

The dreaded ‘pot-pelly pox’ has struck one of our provinces. This disease has long been an endemic scourge of the world, causing fever, malaise, and then the characteristic swelling of the lower abdomen, with the eventual protrusion of pox-like ridges across the skin in this area. It is particularly notable for affecting and killing infants and young children. In ancient times, the pox was construed as a demonic mirror of pregnancy, but in the modern age, it is clear that this is just a pestilence like others. It is not exactly clear what sort of reservoir was host to this illness. Polluted water supplies are the most likely cause. Local officials and clergy members noticed first a collection of orphans showing this illness, and then quickly the elderly, and other vulnerable populations. They have urgently addressed our government seeking support for the quarantining of afflicted regions.

The ‘blinding cough’ has struck one of our provinces. This epidemic is known for its particularly grotesque marring of the throat and eyes, causing these regions to necrotize and the tissue to peel away, hence the appellation ‘blinding cough’. It typically leaves mass disability in its wake, and is rightfully feared. Indeed, those blinded by this pathogen are an ancient motif in art, and ‘cough houses’ are a typical nicknames for institutions designed to host the indigent and disabled paupers in society. As such, this dreadful illness leaves a lasting burden on society, beyond just killing. Public officials first identified it as present in the province by monitoring intake in charity and state run hospitals, with notable sections of the poor displaying the disease progressing to an alarming extent, and have urged the government to take action to prevent the spread of this horrendous illness.

The ‘Cud-Feeder’s Flu’ has struck one of our provinces! This gastrointestinal problem seems to notably afflict those who consume infected thrall-meat (called so from the typical reliance of ruminant hominids as thralls), causing malaise, confusion, and dysentery. Doctors believe that the practice of letting thralls ‘grub’ in the scrublands for their subsistence of roots, grasses, and insects, exposes them to pathogens in the humus. The chronic maltreatment of thralls means that sick and weak thralls are often merely culled and sold early, before they can themselves die of the disease. There was likely some sort of infected meat present in this region, and now the bacterium is flourishing throughout our population, for it seems to be able to spread through water supplies as well. Medical experts in the area suggest that the government establish a cordon sanitaire to prevent transmission to further regions, and indeed thrall keeper cartels are eagerly lobbying the government to prevent the spread.

The main problem our colonial administrators have in our lands in colonial Shobgizob is the persistent bloodletting done by the Kusii faithful. Despite efforts to forbid this practice, they still continue to maintain clandestine meetings at the officially proscribed temples and kill large amounts of animals and even people, which is a serious impediment to colonial governance, an insult to our laws, and generally a waste of the population resources of the state. Our current governor, in an effort to properly enforce the laws which forbid their cult (which have largely been ignored out until now out of practical necessity in not enraging a colonial populace), has submitted a report to $CAPITAL$, requesting permission to forcibly engage a detachment of sailors and soldiers to be employed in the dismantlement of their ghastly temple complexes, and to pay a scholar to study their strange faith in an effort to understand what drives them to this bloodshed.

Before heading eastward to the border stations in Sem, there has to be a decision made on what to offer in exchange for Rannutan facilitation of Dehuogi migration. This is to be our bid to get them to comply, but of course they can refuse and we will keep our offer. We must keep in mind that if the Rannutan have state serfs to give, they will likely send us far more souls.

We have just received a deputation from the Bogoran lands with the most curious proposal. The ministers of state are meeting in conclave before producing a reply to the Bogorans. They have proposed that we deport a large amount of the Dehuogi of the east of the empire to Bogoran lands, where they will become privileged settlers. The Dehuogi are a perennial thorn in our side - their horrendous Hajduks and bandits claim to serve the deposed pretenders of House Budobam, a puppet of the Vokonazhi, and the average Dehuogi brute drags his feet through every command. Whether we sent them a collection of troublesome serfs, or cleared out some artisan settlements, it would give us more certain control of this troubled region, though the prospect of deportations is sure to engulf the region in anger. The Bogorugi have patiently put this request before us.

The talks we began with the Imperial Court of the Rannutan Empire about the invitation of their Dehuogi settlers into our lands have apparently faltered, with our diplomats arriving this morning dejected and gloomy. They are expected to give a full address to the assembly of clans this afternoon, but the interior ministry considers the matter a forgone conclusion: Rannutan has no interest.

The talks we began with the Imperial Court of the Rannutan Empire about the invitation of their Dehuogi settlers into our lands have been successful! We had only scarcely received the diplomats themselves at a border post, who had been gone for about two months, when they informed us that coming shortly behind them were a beleaguered line of Dehuogi who had been marched across the empire with a Rannutan Imperial Army Escort. These settlers are complaining of great mistreatment at the hands of the Rannutan, and are in quite poor condition, having left with only their pack animals and what goods they could carry, but seem eager at the prospect of the large acres we have set aside for them in one of the least governed lands at the western edge of our state. The government has already made contact with a few community leaders to begin establishing their clan government, granted them their banner, and provided them with some Oujoy bearers.
Our state, nay - our people, are strengthened today.

English: It has become clear that our state is bereft of a clear constitution. Various authorities, documents, laws, and powers create a terrible muddle, and the state is inefficient and disorganised. The government has directed that a new series of major laws be drafted to determine the constitutional direction of our country. Leading luminaries and politicians have gathered to debate this issue, but it’s unsettled as to what sort of constitution is to have: one with a higher degree of central authority, or one with a higher degree of devolved powers?

Our recent government initiative to abolish serfdom has not gone down well in the provinces. Enraged landowners have declared that their ancient and ancestral rights are being trampled upon by an out of control government. Many of them have formed seditionist leagues, gathering antique weapons, saddling their swines, and declaring that if the abolition is brought to their estates, they will resist the government. The army has declared that it is willing to enforce the government’s will by means of arms, but many in the legislature are nervously muttering if it is really worth it. While many feared that the abolition of the serfdom in our country would cause much resistance, much to the relief of the government, it has gone over with little trouble, barring a little grumbling from the aristocracy and the reactionary circles.

Its arrival is unmistakable: the characteristic hemorrhaging of copious amounts of blood from all orifices, with rapid onset, sometimes in the middle of the street, or in a pale, sweating visitor to a hospital. The Red Flux has arrived in our country, and already in one of our provinces, more and more victims are being struck with this dreadful illness as it rages through our population. Terrified residents are shuttering their windows, doors, and praying that the illness will not strike them, while the coroners direct the corpse wagons to large funerary sites beyond the borders of major towns and settlements. This is, many are saying, the beginning of a grim episode of our nation’s history.

The residents of one of our provinces, briefly, thought a corpse had come to walk! But almost more chillingly, it seems the recent news of an epidemic of wasting sickness has been particularly relevant, as it appears the wasting sickness has spread to one of our provinces! Indeed, the doctors who attempted to treat this victim, and the coroner who attempted to dispose of the corpse once the victim perished, have all come down with this sickening affliction of the skin, causing the flesh to necrotise, and the tissue to peel away, attracting swarming hosts of flies that bite at the rotting flesh. Indeed, the whole province has been thrown into turmoil, with great consternation at the spread of the illness, and many regular activities of life have come to a grinding halt in an effort to avoid the spread of the plague.

The recent terrible pandemic that had struck our lands has finally abated. In all of our districts, life seems to have returned to normal, and while our society is left with many scarred survivors, grieving families, and disrupted life, it seems that most of the populace is now immune to the new strain of the pandemic, having faced the terrible trial of illness themselves, and come through it alive.

English: Bogorug is a large aristocratic commonwealth in the northern reaches of Ishahfazh. The Bogoran state is organised around a system of hereditary clan-castes, all reputedly descended from the Vewugist nomadic clans who came and conquered the lands of now Bogorug in the 530s. They maintain a brutal oppression of the Oujoy people who lived there before their arrival, by a system of castes (the Oujoy are said to belong to the ‘sixth’ clan), a swinebacked noble gendarmerie, and monopolisation of all the land. The clans maintain both justice for their members, headed by a ‘warchief’ and meet in the assembly of the old clans, the Bogoran legislature, where each clan has one vote. Clan membership is a personal hereditary status, through the mother, not a geographic one but there are clusters of clanship.

The northern states of Ishahfazh have a decided flavour of the chivalrous, and the romantic, as opposed to the imperial and the commercial south. The rugged landscapes of the north, riven with great mountains, forests, and dales, has tended to foster societies which are, on the whole, poorer, but also politically and socially more personal. Dominated by large monarchical states, the rituals of kingship, tribute, and sober duty are deeply important to the region, where great kings often invoke ancestral titles, age old submissions, and the doctrines of legitimacy to compete over the variegated kingdoms, peoples, and clans of the north. It is mostly a sedentarian region, but the Bogorugi state is confessionally Vewugist, despite many sedentians in its lower classes. The Rannu Empire, after its gradual absorption or domination of the smaller lordships and kingdoms, has long been at odds with the consolidated kingdom of Mamatoukat, with the Bogorans traditionally siding with the Rannu.

Pruub is a term for the extracted oils gathered from the crushed up Magoupt plant, which is found in the Poudwouvas riverbeds. For millennia it has been chewed, smoked, and lathered on mucous membranes by the people of Poumnia to induce a deeply euphoric state. In the modern world it is a highly popular drug, and often inhaled ‘in the Poumnian style’ after being mixed with water vapors. The bud of the Magoupt plant is famed for being most dense in oils, and is sometimes eaten, despite its bitter taste. The drug is delighted in by many, but above all by the Poumnian and Gashdzii aristocracies, who smoke it nearly continuously, and the royal export monopoly has historically made the Poumnian crown very wealthy.

Nuddi is a relaxing root infusion drink that is drunk in almost all parts of the civilized world. The Nuddi root is harvested and then mashed into a paste, where it is often placed in a communal vat or keg. The infusion has dormitive virtues, and when drunk in large quantities is said to induce strange dreams. It is a popular drink among the lower and middle classes, and ‘Nuddi Houses’, with comfortable poufs and divans are considered the bare essentials of a civilised city. The fibers of the plant are sometimes used to make clothing, especially for the slaves who so often have to dig the roots. The finest Nuddi is said to grow in the Kovan Isles, where it has been planted to great success, where the roots grow to prodigious size. The plant is originally thought to be from Ishahfazh, however.

Nuzhdap is a mild hallucinogenic herb that is ground up and then smoked in long pipes. First discovered smoked by Vuyti by Gashdzii settlers fording into the east of Ishahfazh, it quickly became a popular drug. Upon making its way to the west, the Vewugi faith seized upon it as a source of mystical visions, and they regularly smoke it in hopes of getting a glimpse of their master, the Vewug. The finest Nuzhap is still said to grow in the east, particularly Gizhok, in Gaubja, where some of the oldest plantations and trademarks exist: ‘Golden Dreams’ (Niiz Bollok) and ‘Farmer’s Rest’ (Padudazh Zhim).

Thralldom is a term to refer to the ubiquitous practice in the Miiv of keeping other species of hominids as intelligent cattle. Especially in the more desolate and barren parts of the world and marginal economies of small freeholding peasants, the practice is viewed as not only economically viable but also culturally significant, prized as ‘the finest meat’ and indulged in by many believing the proteins of manflesh are curative to the brain and eyes, and a source of civilizational prosperity. In recent years this idea has come under attack, as either unsanitary, economically wasteful, or barbaric. Thralls are typically raised until about age 15, when they are fattened and then killed.
Here one may find brief descriptions of the continents of the world.

Ishahfazh is the second largest continent in the world, and by far the most politically and economically developed. Ishah-fazh means 'setting sun land', and was originally a Gashdzii word for the west, until it took on greater significance in the early plateau period. Geographically Ishahfazh is divided by a large desert band into a definite north and south, and features a large spine of mountains connecting the two on the western edge of the continent. The south is dominated by vast savannahs, huge river flats, dense jungle, and fetid mangrove swamps. The north, contrarily, is covered in temperate forests, undulating hills, and foggy plains.

Kovazh is the third largest of the continents proper, and is so-called in the Gashzii tongue from the Xouvan people who inhabit its northern coasts. Largely flat and temperate, it is dominated by great steppes, deserts, and plains. Its political history has consequently been dominated by alternating periods of great conflicts and great empires. Despite being full of ancient civilizations and peoples, it remains economically underdeveloped and decentralized.

The great eastern continent, named so by the Gashdzii term for east - ‘Bafa’ - a pre-Kadkohic vengeful sun god. It is the largest of all six major landmasses and also boasts most of the most impressive natural formations. Marked by its primitive stage of development, empty landscapes, vast mountain ranges, deep valleys, and endless forests, it represents at once opportunity and freedom as well as the great unknown.

Shobgizob is a far flung continental shelf in the reaches of the southern oceans. Mainly dominated by two large islands, it features a number of small archipelagos as well. Mountainous and windy, and covered mostly in sparse, temperate forests, the region is home to many grazing animals and large seabirds and a small settlement of culturally homogenous hominids. Currently, the land is wracked by religious strife after the arrival of the Vewugist faith through missionary activity.

‘The Land of the Spears’ (named so either because of its hostile inhabitants or the large horned animals that graze in its cool forests), Paukzhodo is the fourth largest continent or the largest subcontinent in the world. Lying just of the northern coast of Ishahfazh, its own northern coast hugs the great northern sea and is buffeted by brutal storms and cold winds, but its more temperate south is marked by large river complexes populated by fishing, hunting, and farming communities who bring strange pelts and fine timber out of the north.

The smallest of all the legitimate continents, Gofakidzia is one of the most isolated and extreme regions in the world. In the far reaches of the north and amidst the paths of the great storms that rage in the northern seas, it seems a miracle hominids made it there at all. Indeed, the Mjhm'an People who live there speak a strange and barbarous isolate, and live a truly wretched life in this harsh land ruled by great storms.

An aristocratic commonwealth is a term for a common form of government across the world in which the state is dominated by large noble magnates who rule in a quasi-parliamentary regime with a weak monarch or no monarch at all. Various other terms for this government and the movements associated with it would be aristocratic constitutionalism or aristocratic republicanism. It usually features sweeping proprietary and social rights vested in the nobility and clergy, many regional privileges, and highly formalized, ritualized, and documentary political institutions.

Liberationism is a prominent ideological movement in much of the developed world in Ishahfazh. Decrying traditional feudal structures, aristocratic and monarchical tyranny, and lauding agrarian free peasant lifestyles, Liberationism has become a revolutionary movement to create a utopian state for the common people. Liberationists aim to create what could be described as paternalistic agrarian regimes that are oriented to spreading anti-feudal revolution and maintaining demotic welfare policies. Prominent theorists include Yathoon Ifo and Sevu Orooth, who argued for a form a divinely ordained polity guided by a sovereign will manifest in the biological and spiritual vitality of an agent.

A ‘paternalist council’ is a typical term for the form of conciliar government preferred by Liberationists. Generally modeled after the ‘Sublimely Guided Demotic Assembly’ erected by the revolutionary government in what is now Veyethu (the holy state) after the Liberationist uprising of 1297, it typically features appointed or elected ‘tribunes’ who collaborate in a centralized system to direct and control public welfare and military campaigns. Contrary to much of the rhetorical discourse attendant to these governments, they tend to be fairly brutal, narrow in involvement, and antidemocratic. They are in fact intentionally so, their purpose consisting only of maintaining plebeian social (not political) rights and waging war against aristocratic enemies.

A princely despotate is a general term for centralized proprietary states of various forms of dictatorial and monarchical governance across the world. It generally features a lone sovereign or first citizen, surrounded by a coterie of ministers and servants, governing in a fairly arbitrary way, and typically features a fairly strong bourgeois bureaucratic or military establishment to maintain the will of the Prince.

Statism is an ideological and political movement that champions the state as the historic and natural subject of history and society. Citizens are merely subordinate members of a state enterprise, and the pursuit of efficient social and economic management at the expense of all other considerations is the aim of the statist politician. It is in spirit an offshoot of the Azhkazhine functionalist movement, formulated by Shomo Mudt, in the late 1310s, who applied the functionalist ontology to the state and the material world, as well as advocated for secularism, poor relief, and reform of a large variety of kinds. Mudt took the state’s being to be its capacity to act as a state: increase its powers for violence, tax collection, and consent, and advocated for a system of reform to enhance all these things.

Theocratism is a broadly conservative and reactionary movement that seeks to synthesize statist and absolutist methods of social control with reactionary and conservative aims. Seeking to restore traditional social privileges and religious authorities, they are most principally the enemies of liberationists. The origins of the theocratist movement are in the thoughts, writings, and lectures of Deacon Mogga, a radical preacher and paramilitary agitator from the Gozonazh peninsula.

House Budobam is a small and diminutive dynasty reigning on the Island of Kuabtashug, off the coast of northern Vokonazh. Once a major Dehuogi dynasty ruling an ethnically homogeneous proto-national Dehuogi ‘ikui?Bekob’ (Royal Domain) from the 7th to the 10th century, incursions by the Rannu empire let to their progressive collapse. Fleeing to a tributary island, the dynasty persisted, eventually converting to the Kadkohi pantheon and collaborating with the regional power of Vokonazh, who remains a patron. For more than two hundred years, the Budobaman, ‘those of budobam’, have ruled in the Kaubtashug, and continued to claim the allegiance of all the Dehuogi. The Rannutan currently rule most of the Dehuogi lands, and have claimed legitimate mastery of the ‘heathen’ Dehuogi lands in the name of the sedentarian faith, which has been augmented by a series of titles borne by the Rannutan Emperor for many centuries now.

The Rannu empire is a large and old Tehuhrite empire which dominates the northern reaches of Ishahfazh. Emerging from a collection of allied tribute taking military castes in the north of the continent, the martial Unnahu and Unnobanhu peoples slowly spread their influence around the region, dominating local upland tribes, neighbouring people and establishing sturdy borderlands. The pressures of modernisation caused this vaguely unstable network of warlords to gradually sacralise and institutionalize a tradition of imperial administration by regional governorates organised by local, loyal elites. The central point of the Rannu Empire is the Rannutan Dynasty, which gradually assumed greater power during the early 8th century as the power of the Bennaru faded. Dynastic submission by compliant local governors, trained in Tehuhrite philosophy, which sanctions the entire regime as an order-bringing empire.

He was found, stumbling up to the hospital gates, wheezing and coughing, yellow-white pus collecting like spittle at the edges of both his mouth and nose, pleading for help. The doctors did their best to treat him, but in the end his pus filled lungs gave out, and he died in his hospital bed. He was not the first, and he will not be the last. The terrible pandemic of ‘white flux’ seems to have arrived in one of our provinces, spreading like wildfire, and striking old and young alike. Distressed city officials have decreed a few belated quarantines, but it seems to do little to stop the spread of a disease that seems to pervade the very air, an unwholesome miasama, and the citizenry themselves shutter their doors and windows, while the sick stumble around the city, coughing, banging on doors, and pleading for help.

Despite all our best efforts, the cordon sanitaire of our capital has failed! The ghastly pandemic now stalks the streets of $CAPITAL$, and the soldiers deployed to enforce the quarantines are themselves ill with the accursed gripe! There is no point now in sinking such resources into the maintenance of the quarantine system.

With the outbreak of military conflict, it has become, for all intents and purposes, untenable to maintain our cordon sanitaire implemented in our capital to protect against the alarming spread of the global pandemic. We can no longer sanction the diversion of military resources to maintenance of district checks at the capital, and furthermore, it is expected that the cycling of units back and forth from the frontline for recuperation and medication, as well as for supply and resupply, if the war persists, will make cordon saintaire superfluous. Doubtless, too, the possible arrival of foreign soldiers, refugees, and other incidents of war means altogether we must brave the possibility of disease as well as occupation!
We have a more pressing use for the military now.

We have received news, through the various Vewugist missionary societies, that the political and social elite of $FROMCOUNTRY$ have, undoubtedly under the guidance of the very same pious Vewugist missionaries, converted to Vewugism! This is unmistakably a wonderful day for the hosts of his majesty and might the holy Vewug, as it is his pleasure to see his faithful increasing, for our puny souls go someway to endow him with the power to secure us with ever greater favours and boons, and reign down misfortune on our enemies. Though they are quite primitive, these pagans in $FROMCOUNTRY$ are clearly on the path to civilization.

In the Shau Zhakd, the ‘new settlements’ of the western coast of Bafozh, for several decades a collection of Gashdzii settlers lived largely ungoverned by any state system. Unlike the Kushnâg or Poponazh, the abundance of land and the relative placid nature of the Fauwozhi seems to have given rise to a remarkably communitarian and voluntarist political structure, if it can be called a political structure at all. Now, however, since we have established our dominion over these lands, the local Jazhakdi have been complaining of the arbitrary and wanton trampling of their ancient privileges. In any sense of the formal Gashdzii political and religious legal tradition, they are indeed nearly totally beyond it. However, a collection of them have submitted a request to formalise what they call the ‘Zhakdnâg’ or the ‘setter/farmer concern/public matter.’ This decentralised intuition would be under our protection, and would guarantee us their goodwill.
Rifts Emerge in the New Government!

The Gaubjan state was wracked in the mid 1270s by a particularly bloody palace coup against the old dynasty. The Pozâfauk Dynasty was overthrown and house Bodimhazh came to the throne, making the beheading of old Mozzanak II Pozâfauk their very flag. By all accounts, too, his young son, Mozzanimiz IV, was killed as well, but this did not stop a number of popular uprisings to be organised in the support of various pretenders who claimed to be Nimiz in the 1270s and 80s, largely an expression of popular discontent with the royal regime, and proto-liberationist notions. The recent Free Yoker revolution drew much of its support from groups organised in support of the various ‘false’ Nimizk, and now, it seems, the governing council is divided. A large contingent wish to restore the Pozâfauk dynasty, and aspects of the old constitution, but other, more ideological yokers, denounce these ambitions as a betrayal of the revolution.

The Maabizhpti Peninsula is hardly a peninsula, but the large jutting out from the Ishahfazhi mainland that hosts the great states of Gaubja and Jiishanâg. Named ‘the cut lands’ from the practice of slash and burn farming by the settlers of the area, this part of the world was the furthest reaches of the ancient Kiidnazh, with the first Gashdzii settlements beginning in the 500s. The region is marked by the continual colonial expansion of the Gashdzii states at the expense of the Vuyti speaking peoples of the jungles and plains, and the simultaneous jockeying and aggression between the four principal Gashdzii states in the region, above all between the Kingdom of Gaubja and the Jiishanâgi commonwealth, who still also profess nominal loyalty to the Kiidnazhk in Pashdzii, unlike the newer settler states of Gozonazh and Chiishozd.

The creation of a Uttonbanhu state beyond our borders has been a disaster for our state. The ancient nature of our government as a confederation of military nobles means that much of the identity of local peoples is tied to a sense of loyalty to local aristocrats. Aristocratic identification with this state, their citation of the ‘organic transference of the ancient common constitution of the Uttobanhu nation’ to the new state of Bennareth, has driven the people into a sense of noncompliance, and dramatically impaired the functioning of both local and national governance of the Uttobanhu people within our borders.

For some time in recent history the Uttobanhu state of Bennareth has maintained pretentious independence from our empire, while we were weakened and unable to maintain control over these regions. Now, we have recovered the lost lands of Bennareth, and the government has seen it as prudent to re-enroll the old Uttobanhu families in the register of the imperial parliament. It is hoped that this will go someways to reestablishing consent to governance over these lands, resurrecting the ancient compact that was the basis of our state, and drawing the Uttobanhu elite again into the fold of the Rannu empire.
Back under the yoke with you lot.

The belonging of the Ngoghu people to our state was always tenuous. Despite efforts to include them in our governance, they have consistently dragged their feet in cooperating with our state. Now, however, with the creation of the artificial state of ‘Vadobeth’, the Ngoghu have seemingly erupted in an outpouring of national fervor, their poets and intelligentsia rejoicing at the supposed ‘liberation’ of their state from our apparently tyrannical rule. Doubtless this is artificial ethnogenesis, organised by the many enemies of the Rannutan, but regrettably it has caused much difficulties in effecting compliance of the Ngoghu populations who remain within our borders.

For some time in recent history, the altogether false state known as ‘Vadobeth’, doubtlessly propped up by the many enemies of the ancient Rannu empire (indeed, it is well known that this region was teeming with Gashdzii and Oujoys), we had suffered to allow independence, but now it has again been integrated in our empire. The Ngoghu, to whom some years ago we condescended to allow representation in our governance, have come grovelling back to us, requesting their old privileges. The imperial officialdom has generously allowed this, acknowledging that the simple Ngoghine were easily deceived into rebellion and disloyalty. A number of oaths of fealty have been extracted from the Ngoghine aristocracy, and Vadobeth is once again a geographic subdivision of the great Rannu Empire!
Back under the yoke with you lot.

Since the great revolution of 1297, our state has been the foremost liberationist state in the world. We have led the charge against the bastions of nobility, privilege, and aristocratic tyranny, and kept the yoke of both the factory and of serfdom away from the vital menfolk of our land… or so the story of the government's official orators goes. But many are rather grumbling that in fact, the government has not so much preserved the spirit of the revolution, but gradually settled into a conservative complacency, an embrace of statist revisionary thought, and ultimately a betrayal of the revolutionary virtues of 1297. In a particularly stark denunciation in the governing councils chambers, extreme liberationist ideologues decried the current government’s policies as aristocratic in nature, and cried out for a new age of vitalistic renewal, decamping en-masse from the chamber!
The End of the Dumuv System?

The recent actions by the imperial government to abolish the system of beneficiaries and banalities owed to the state and the nobles by the vast majority of the common people in Poumnia has caused a massive uproar across the land. Not only does the majority of our country rely on this system for most of its economic production, throwing many provinces into chaos and recession, but this ancient practice is one of the most basic foundations of our state. The military aristocracy, whose private domains blend with regional government, are justifiably furious, with a large part of their jurisdiction and an important source of wealth taken away. It remains to be seen how this affects our country, but many parts of the imperial clergy are suggesting perhaps that the scope of the project of liberation and reform should be limited.
A Vessel for the World Soul

When a new Pudwou ascends the throne, he is expected to hold a great marriage ceremony where noble houses swear fealty and assert the emperor’s divine status, and the Emperor is married to hundreds of noblewomen from these houses. In the coming months, before any wife gives birth to children, the Pudwou is expected to consult his ancestors (the mummified past Pudwous) to decide which wife will give birth to his new heir. This decision must be made before the child is born, so the mother can undergo the divination ritual where her womb is blessed and imbued with the Pudwou’s spiritual power. Since the quieting of the previous Pudwou some days ago, the new embodiment of the world soul has summoned his many nobles to Prousorum for such a ritual. But the question remains of which wife to select for such a role: despite its spiritual significance, it often has a bearing on the fortunes of the noble house which is selected. As often happens, a great house is vying with a particularly capable small house.

Our government, state, and society has gradually taken on a remarkably distinct character. Both large scale decentralisation and federalisation, as well as the gradual enshrinement of common usufruct and voluntarist collectivism as a parallel legal system to the ‘watchman’ oriented civil apparatus, has begotten a unique constitution where regionalism, pastoralism, village collectivism, are the order of the day. Our state is a patchwork of various communes, workingmen's traveling artels, and mutual covenants to maintain infrastructure, bonded by a number of treaties and pacts, and the force of almighty tradition and independent courts, and may be rightly described, in the common parlance, as a ‘pastoral confederacy’.
Truly, this is a worldly utopia.

The gradual centralisation of power in the hands of a few capable autocrats, as well as the gradual enshrinement of commoning laws, and ultimately the autonomy of the landholding legal system from the civil law, means our country has taken on the character, broadly, of the paradigmatic Liberationist state. Finally, and perhaps inevitability, it has happened that the government has declared the suspension of regular parliamentary activities, and established a directorate council, chaired by a rotating ‘Lord Protector’, to guarantee the constitution. This transition has happened entirely peaceably, given that, barring the formal change, our constitution has effectively operated like this for some time.
Through absolute unity only can the common will be found and secured!

The gradual concentration of land tenure into large scale collectivised real property units, coupled with the progressive decentralisation of government into a broadly corporatist system of administration, means our state-society matrix has taken on a unique character. Citizens tend, in fact, to own very little property themselves, but belong to large industrial syndicates and guilds, craft-cities, or industrialized agrarian units, where they work and receive a wage according to a strict hierarchy of obedience and progress. These various collective farms, city organisations, industrial firms, universities, maintain a strong degree of autonomy from each other (while usually maintaining highly stratified authoritarian relations internally), have gradually organised themselves into a syndicate of syndicates of syndicates. The grand syndicate meets regularly to determine an organised policy, and set state-wide concerns and objectives, which are binding to all syndicates.
Prudence, obedience, and production are the guarantors of social stability and safety.

The gradual concentration of all state power into the hands of a number of professional bureaucrats, as well as the large scale collectivisation of agriculture and the gradual abolition of the rural landholding class and the village system, means that our government has increasingly taken on a character amenable to and approved of by the statist parties of our nation. It is not surprising, then, that the official roles of collective farm director, and other members of the administrative secretariat, has attracted statist minded citizens, despite our best efforts at ideological screening. It appears that the statist parties have long been organising a parallel administration, coordination policy just as much in meetings of the statist party as well as in the bureaucratic chambers and the parliament. In a bloodless coup, the statist party, in conjunction with a number of senior bureaucrats, have annulled the current session of parliament, and proclaimed a new constitution.
The resolutions of the party are all that are between us and anarchic collapse.

$FROMCOUNTRY$, one of our neighbours, seems to be experiencing extreme upheaval. Wracked by rebels and civil war, we learn every day of new atrocities by the rebels, and refugees trickle across our borders to escape the chaos, as soldiers maraude the land, requisitioning food and supplies from villages, and massacring those who resist. As we are guarantors of order and tradition, the beleaguered government has appealed to us, citing a solidarity in tradition, legitimacy, reaction, and regional stability, asking us to aid in the effort to defeat the rebels. They will certainly be grateful to us if we do.
We must stamp out revolution wherever it rises!
The $FROMCOUNTRY_ADJ$ are on their own in this matter

It is well known that the Parqmun sculpt small wooden idols of various demons and spirits, and then burn them in great holocausts, to honour Mun and destroy the power of the devils and spirits. But one of our anthropological professors, who spent a number of years living with the Parqmun, has recently compiled a great degree of observations about the character of the idols, and compared them to catalogs of the idols held by the juewaeg faithful kept in the archives and private scholarly libraries in $CAPITAL$, drawing notable similarities. He has come up with a particularly fascinating thesis that a number of more powerful Parqmum empires once ruled a much larger area in Bafozh, and came across, and came to understand, the horrendous sacrificial rites happening in the southern forests, and because of this came to identify this particular style of idol with devilish activity.
The Grave Stele of Knagtka Kneg?

Upon our occupation of Knutsk, we have found a fascinating scene. A towering stele on the top of a large hill, with deep relief engravings depicting the sun, a man, and a number of his deeds, as well as, it appears, his birth from the sun. Many nomadic peoples seemingly have come many thousands of miles to place small trinkets, flags, and other precious items at the foot of this huge stele. The local colonial officer began asking the local people who had erected this stele, what was it for, and why was it here. After some difficulties, they explained this is the gravesite of Knagtka Kneg, the prophet of the Dkatkang faith, and was erected on the order of the Prince of Nan Tsetk, who rules many hundreds of miles to the north. The Stele features his birth as an incarnation of the sun, his itinerant labours and miracles, during his life, and the eventual passing away of this body, his promise to send another prophet, and his reunion with the sun.

The Pruunts are the Diwvish speaking people living on the southern Reuhriz peninsula of Ishahfazh. They are a seafaring people, and related in tongue and race to the Poumnians, the Roshupt, and the Towuzhans. However, their cultural identity is far different. While the stolid Poumnians developed an imperial, rural culture, the Pruunts were some of the first urbanists, founding small social-military city communities millennia ago, and developing a unique ethno-religious tradition of Shamush. Gradually, Pruuntia came under the sway of Imperial Poumnia, who made the Pruuntish states tributaries of the Vopudwou, and injected the Pruuntish tongue with much Poumnianism, and somewhat feudalised their society, but the urbanism, religious mysticism, and stubbornness persists in Pruuntia. The Pruuntish elite is divided into the imperialists, who pay their respects at the imperial temples, and the Pruuntics, who attend sermons of the Shamushic teachers.

The western Gashdzii lands are the area where the Gashdzii dialect is most pure, the traditions of the Gashdzii are the most unalloyed. The Gashdzii’s origins are from those of warlike swine-riding nomad clans. Historically they were a fiercely proud and independent people interconnected through vast familial ties. The culture of steppe-riders still marks this now long sedentary society even in contemporary ages, and many of their cultural signs like thigh-slapping are from this era. The West Gashdzii tend to prefer to live in the great plateaus of this region, in stone houses with fine courtyards, and they are the most urban of the Gashdzii. Despite this, many of the common folk live in small stone and mud houses on the great savannah and riverbeds. They mostly eat breads mainly from hardy savannah grains, as well as the meat of their swine and great aurochs that graze in the savannah. The red robe is a traditional noble dress, with most states forbidding non-aristocrats from donning it.

The south Gashdzii mostly live in the coastal and plains regions of the ‘newer’ settlements of their empire. While they have many proud cities and are a very mercantile people, the majority are actually farmers, a continuing legacy of their settler past. Their language takes more borrowings from the Poumnian, as well as Vuyti, and they tend to speak a far more demotic language than that of the stilted west or laconic north. Despite this, their culture, in some ways, preserves a greater austerity and somberness than the ‘decadent’ aristocrats of the west or the barbarous generals of the north, for the southern Gashdzii are deeply steeped in the austere purity and fierce sense of justice of the Motkohnic faith, and their sober dress, tidy cities, and exacting agrarian landlords are famous. They, like the rest of the Gashdzii, enjoy a diet largely of grains, fruit, and large cattle animals that are raised on the plains and savannah.

The North Gashdzii are a warrior people, nearly all in the old ‘Vokonazh’, the eastern borderlands, where the Duyo and the Eshemi pastoralists were driven from with much difficulty. The Vokonazh used to be a violent and bloody realm, and the culture of the North keeps to this legacy. Largely settled in great serf-estates, organised to support a military lord, the tradition of noble officers leading their bonded men into battle, and the military virtues associated with this, permeate North Gashdzii society. It is no wonder that the Kadkohi deity Doshk, of the dry season, of death, of loss, and pain, as well as order and stillness, ‘the austere father’, is the preferred deity of most of the ruling dynasties, who attempt to cultivate a society of obedience and order in a harsh landscape. North Gasdhzii culture is also bound up with fidelity to the Midodazh dynasty, the ancient lords of the Vokonazh, and it is not uncommon for peasants to keep a picture of the current prince.

The Sithevan people are a belt of common ethnolinguistic identity along the western edge of southern Ishahfazh. The Central Sithevan dialects are generally mutually intelligible, but remain culturally differentiated by a history of different historic ruling dynasties, different lifestyles (the pastoral north, the agrarian south), different cultural contacts, occupations, and subsequent different legal traditions (Towuzhian, Poumnian, Ghech). The experience of being ruled by the great, ancient Athisoron dynasty, however, has driven them into a consciousness of a common history. The Chyothit, the Tufume, and the Vufami, all living much further afield, having adopted different faiths, different lifestyles, and constitutions, never experienced the homogenizing influence of the Athisoron dynasty.

The Central Sithevans are all those tongues and cultures that spoke a Sithevan language, and experienced the homogonising rule of the house of Athis. The Sithevan people were, over a millenia ago, a disorganized collection of military tribes broadly in the tribute of either the Poumnians or lorded over by the Ghech. Sitheve was far less of an identity, but rather an etic term for a cluster of peoples. The Vewugist developments in the 400s greatly strengthened Sithevan identity, and the early Vewugist kingdoms ruled for around 200 years before collapsing. The Rise of house Athis in the 700s once again brought a consolidated Sithevan to the world, but which had to contend with the regionalism of the Ghech-ruled Thes and Sevuma, and the Poumnian influenced Hahabi. The Hahuibi consider themselves the ‘purest’ expression of Sithevan culture, and its ‘good natured’ roots in the free tribes who settled around lake Chyufov, but the Hahabi consider themselves more sophisticated, the Sevuma themselves more pious, etc.

The Vufami are a sithevan culture living in the southern reaches of Ishahfazh. Transplanted there after the great Vewugist migrations, they have largely adopted to the local lifestyles, tilling the jungle soils for starchy roots, living in tower-cities on the plains, in the mashes, and in the jungles, and even have taken to birding, like the elites of Toworud. Nonetheless, they remain committed to their Vewugist faith, and continue to be highly conscious of the linguistic difference between them and their neighbours. There is only one Vufami state, the monarchy of Chyivit, with which both the Poumnians and the Pruunts acknowledge as the legitimate protector of Vewugists in the Poumnian Empire. The garbled and ancient dialect, as well as their stark poverty, makes the Vufami an object of interest for most sithevans, a sort of ‘living relict’ of their ancient conquesting past, but not totally alien like the Tufume or Chyothit.

The Tufume are the Island Sithevans. Having arrived in the Takemogi isles in the 400s, they have gradually adopted the lifestyle of these people, even moving into the weather resistance fortresses they live in, and mostly converting to sedentarian traditions and abandoning their Vewugism. The linguistic issue remains conscientious, as the Takemogi crown, resenting the tongue of the ancient invaders, has tried variously to curb it, grant concessions, or avoid dealing with it all together. The ancient kingdom of Gibumovon is still a fond memory for highly particularist Tufume, but altogether they are mostly quiescent subjects of the Takemogi crown, who see them as a regrettable quirk of history that’s confined to a small region. They, like the Takemoujoy, subsist largely on fish and break, as well as the occasional flank of cattlemeat.

The Surgoian peoples are a class of various ethnolinguistic communities living in the north west of Ishahfazh. From the Oujoys of the mountains, who share a nearly common tongue, but who have gradually adopted divergent identities due to the rule of the Bogorans over the Yamoujoy, to the oppressed Miegpaup nomads of the deserts, the Gopza of the mountains, and the Islanders of Takemog, a common linguistic root means there is a consciousness of common history, but a variety of different lifestyles and historical differences means these cultures have much variety. ‘Surgoian peoples’ takes its name from the ancient kingdom of Surgoia, which existed c. 100-500 I.R., but there were people of an ancient Surgoian tongue living in this region long before the kingdom, which merely gave rise to its ‘classical’ expression and still is the root of the high culture of Oujoy peoples, whose ancient name, but not culture, gradually has extended to the Takemoujoy, and the Miegpaup.

The Mamoujoy are considered the ‘highest’ expression of Surgoian culture. After the collapse of the Kingdom of Surgoia, they were fractured into many small principalities, but they maintained the traditions and ancient regalia of the court. They are a settled people, depending mostly for their livelihoods on agriculture, forestry, and silkworm harvesting. Most of their homes are wooden, and their cities are known for their intricately carved wooden buildings, with elegant pavilions, carved posts, boards, and inlays, depicting many motifs of Sedenarian philosophy and faith. Their fine, flowing robes are well praised by the people of the world. The nobility of Mamatoukat continue to wear the steel plating of the older-ages, given an extreme attachment to tradition and their ancient privileges. Their society, like most Sedenatian societies, is highly stratified, with the common folk having little allowance to move and resettle, and the institution of serfdom is prolific.

The Yamoujoy, the ‘short brother people’, are the northern mainland Oujoys. They have long been ruled by the Vewugist Bogorans, and as such: their dialect borrowed from the stilted, laconic tongue of the Bogorans, their began to organise their society in terms of clanship and hetmanship, and they take to a martial and pastoral lifestyle far easier than the Mamoujoy or the Takemogine. Despite this, they remain fiercely attached to Sedentarianism, keeping regular routes for their transhumance and cattle driving, and always wintering in the same place. They enjoy an impression of the Tehuhrite faith that emphasises harmony, balance, the flow of a river, and the idea of return. They tend to dress, as well, not in the fine, calming, silk robes of the Mamoujoy, but in more rugged leather outfits and caps, like the Bogorans. They are also great tea-growers, and some say they are the originators of the tea drinking practice.

The Takemoujoy, the ‘military people’, a name they took, it is believed, from their feudal tradition of bonded warfare in service of a local king, are the isular Surgoians. The islands are known for their harsh weather and their dour, self-disciplined people living in great fortresses. The sedentarian faith arrived in the islands long ago, but the Takemogine are looked down upon by most mainland Sedentarians as not truly pious (for how, the theologians in Tauje say, did one get to the island? Surely, he and his kin must have moved there, and forsaken their homeland!). Perhaps consequently, they maintain a less philosophical and more animist version of the faith, venerating island deities of salt and storm, and local mountain and river spirits, and are great seafarers. The people mostly subsist on fish caught in trawlers, island grains, and the meat of the astouding ‘Takemog cattle’, whose shaggy coats and colossal size protect them from cold weather as they graze on the abundant grass of Takemog.

The Meigpaup are the Surgoian nomads of the south Vazzunak peninsula. Nominally sedentarian, they more often than not are close to simplistic animistic theists, worshiping earth and sky and honouring little the teachings of the sages and the philosophers. There are very little of them left, having been driven from Geswoup and Meigtas by the Mamoujoy kingdom and its ‘properly sedentian’ settlers, they live usually in the harsh deserts of this region, eating the meat of the small woolen ruminants the keep, and largely avoiding the government, singing ancient songs.

The Chyothit are the great thrall lords of the Hid Sasoth (The Kingdom of Sasoth), the monarchy of the lower Dhumuh mountains. A clan of sithevans arrived in this region during the Vewugist conquests, and has gradually converted the locals into a most wretched and oppressed people, farmed in great thralllands in the mountain scrubland, or hinterland steppe. The common people of the Chyothit, to little care by the great nobles, are entirely dependent on the Gashdzii merchants of Dhamapaha, who pay them to mine iron for the east-west trade. The Chyothit are known as brutal slavers, wild, inbred, barbarous Sithevans, with disgusting manners, and a decided taste for manflesh. In all likelihood, they are the closest people to the ancient Sithevans who were a persistent trouble for the Poumnians, and well known to the Ghechan war-parties.

The Duttphti are a a linguistic bundle in northern Ishahfazh, their primary representative cultures being the Ûttôbânhu, the Unnahu, the Ngoghu, the Pû?urê and the Yattâe. Primarily incorporated in Rannu Empire, the Ûttôbânhu, the Unnahu, especially, and the Ngoghu to a lesser extent, share a high degree of mutual intelligibility, whereas the Pû?urê and the Yattâe diverged many centuries ago after migrations to Paukzhodo. The Rannuiac folk are known for their staid and somber morality, whereas the wild Pû?urê and Yattâe are known as bold warriors, drinkers, and adventurers, tinged with the paganism of Paukzhodo.

The Unnahu refers to a large cluster of dialects and sedentarian traditions that lie on the northern coast of Ishahfazh. Largely associated with the Rannu empire, as the Rannutan dynasty themselves speak an Unnahu dialect, they nonetheless have a number of distinguishing features that mark them out from their neighbours. A strong, nucleated state centred around the tribute taking dynasties that establish themselves after the arrival of Sedentarianism helped to demarcate them from the Ngoghu on the east coast, whose settlement alongside proto-dehuogi clansmen left them a far more garbled people, while Unnahu high culture began to develop along the northern coasts, rooted in Sedentarian teachings, and highly litigious, their sedentarian ‘rootsmen’ and the gentleman lawyers of Vepht spilling our continuous treatises on the intricacies of tributary and sedentarian law. They are highly agrarian, as well as alcoholic, making ‘bark mash’ from the soft, sugary bark of the Dekh tree.

The Uttobanhu like to pride themselves that they are the most ancient peoples of Northern Ishahfazh. It is very likely that Osju^nne^t of Gohn-Peth, the founder of the Sedentarian faith, spoke a language not far from Uttobanhu now, given their tradition of reading his scriptures in the original, and the continuous affinity for Pethian dramas. It is also the Pethians that adopted the letters of the Poumnians to a Duttuphti language, and which the Uttobanhu continue to use despite the imperial alphabetical reforms of the Unnahu. Much of the original lands of the Uttobanhu have been lost to the Vewugist desert folk, the Bogoran conquerors, and the practical Unnahu, but the Uttobanhu remain, lost in a classical memory of the great kingdoms of the ancient Pethians. They cultivate grains around the coast, and allow great herds of cattle to graze out in Ngogo desert, and usually live in large, low, wooden homes.

The Ngoghu are broadly those Duttuphti peoples living in the region of Vadobeth, the area of land long ruled by the Dehoug when they were both pagan nomads and after they converted to Vewugism. A gradual trickle of settlers from Unnahu regions, (then all calling themselves Dutupht) tricked into these regions to settle and cultivate it, and it was in such a state that the Ngoghu were found as the Unnahu-Uttobanhu imperial complex pushed into this territory. Ngoghu identity is somewhat uncertain, with many speaking a Ngoghu register as well as fine Unnahu, but there is decidedly something regionalist and independent of the Rannu dominion that persists in the attitudes of these people.

The Yattae and the Pugure are the Sedentarian and Duttuphti people who live in the wild of southern Paukzhodo. It is not known exactly when they settled here, but it must have been quite long ago, as their language is far different. It is speculated that they were settlers like the Ngoghu who went further. Nonetheless, now, they live a simple life of fishing, hunting, trapping, logging, and farming in what seasons allow it, while driving away the savage Ogrehi. They are the main point of contact between the goods of Paukzhodo and the traders of more developed nations.

The Huighan tongues, it was a great surprise for the linguists, are all related, from the Unaian monks, to the Bogoran lords, the swineriders of Budobaman, and the oppressed Eshemi and Duyo. Despite great differences between them, nonetheless, they all come from a shared linguistic root, but these cultures share little between them besides language.

The Vuyti peoples are a collection of tri-special peoples living in the southeastern jungles and plains of the Ishahfazh. Divided into plains Paguyti, Jungle Vupuyti, and Üytophat, the Gashdzii-derived slave-soldier-custodian folk. They are renowned for their animism, fertility rituals, and strange war masks. Quite curiously, the Vuyti are an example of cross-species linguistic continuity. The Paguyti are classical ruminoids - fat, plump, gullible, and docile grazers, whereas the Vupuyti are clever semi-arboreal pygmy arboraloids, who display a remarkable intelligence, much greater than the Paguytin. It is assumed that the ancient Vupuyti actually shared the gift of language with the Paguyti through example, whether through primitive exchange, ‘animal’ husbandry - the thralldom of the Paguyti, or by simply chatting around those they deemed disinterested animals while on a journey to the plains. The Paguyti themselves taught their tongue to the Sapinoid Üytophat, the purpose bred, clever 'custodians' of Paguyti society.

The Thihudian peoples are rugged folk who live along the vast central stretch of Ishahfazh - its central deserts (the Zatgibzob, the Ishahgizob, the Dhugheth) and arid mountain spine of the Dhumuh mountains. They are divided regionally, with the Ihtithot in the southern deserts, the Ihnthedehert in the northern deserts, and the Inpihmi and Ihnpedi in the mountain ranges. The desert folk are known for their nomadic lifestyle and terse speech, these people cross the lands with strange pack animals. The mountain folk are known for carrying precious and intricate metalwares mined in secluded mountain valleys, and for their fierce hostility to outsiders. They largely subsist on a diet of pack-animal mutton, fruit, and hardy seed-grains. They are all pygmy arboraloids, like the Vupuyti. It is unclear what drove them to this region in ancient prehistory.

The Dehuogi, once a proud race of nomads, now have been reduced, through the influence of the Rannutan, to a most wretched state. The Rannutan empire has forbidden access to most of their traditional swineriding and grazing lands, and gradually, out of necessity, they have been converted to an agricultural people, toiling on great estates owned by absentee landlords living in Vepht. Many centuries ago, however, they were great nomad pastoralists, and still adorn their bodies with the bones of swine and cattle as they did then. They are generally Vewugists, but a number of the Budobaman elite have converted to Kadkohi through the influence of Vokonazh. Most Dehuogi attempt to identify with the great beasts of the plains, and many cultural rituals relate to borrowing the symbolic might of these animals, or emulating them in some way.

The Bogorans are the Vewugist conquerors who live in northern Ishahfazh. They arrived sometime in the 500s, and have long maintained a violent dominion over the local Oujoys. Their society is organised into five great clans, with a Hetman who regulates both social and political affairs. They are natural born swineriders, and many of the Bogorugi join the clan gendarmes and range across the northern vales policing Oujoy serfs. The cultural sign of the Bogoran elite is the black woolen cap, which is to be worn by adult Bogoran men, and is not to be worn by the Oujoy. Their preferred instrument is the long ‘fashug’, which is a soft wind instrument, a traditional implement of the herdsmen of their society for commanding the woolen ruminants without alarming them, and they are famous for their winsome melodies that echo through the vales of Bogorug.

The people of Kovazh are variegated to a significant degree, both in race, culture, and habits. To the east, there are the imperial Momurist cultures, who have to a varying degree been exposed to incarnations of the large empires that have ruled eastern Kovazh since time immemorial. These people are usually a mix of small cobaloids or sturdy corpuloids. In the north there are the Rechktist warlords and tribesmen, including the Xaeve people, who give their name in ‘Kova’, the Gashdzii interpretation, to the whole continent. To the south and west there are generally found the various vewugist cobaloid ‘tea coasters’ and the feroxaloid savages of the interior.

The ‘Imperial’ cultures of Kovazh are largely those cultures which have been exposed to the various Momurist dynasties for the past few hundred years. They include the Humabi, Tingi, Teong, Dexun, Babi, Soxuppapi, Kwargoi, Rozhyu, and Aucubhur. They are known for their dour moods, contrasted with their shiny gemstones worn in reminder of the ‘purity’ of the Momurist ethic. An interesting custom that has emerged in these cultures is the tradition of ‘male marriage’. Men are expended to marry other men, but still reproduce with female concubines. Male marriages are usually important political and economic alliances, and society is, consequently, even more misogynistic than more cultures in the Miiv, though expectedly more tolerant of male homosexuality.

The northern Kovans are the Biori, the Bhukhegi, and the Kova/Xaeve. They are largely Rechktist nomads, and sometimes are tributaries of the great Momurist empires, but usually try to avoid this. They are all corpuloid hominids beyond the Bhukhegi (who are cobaloids), with sturdy bodies and a glabrous paucity of hair follicles, well suited to trekking across the deserts. The Kova have been subjected to brutal slavery by the Poumnians, who conquered them in the 800s, and have made them into a class of plantation slaves for the production of Nuddi.

The Tea-Coast cultures refer to a variety of cultures and types of hominids found on the west coast of Kovazh. From the elegant Chobajhi, the little cobaloid men in small yellow caps, to the Bofungi of the Khanate and Coebeji of the Kanate, they are all united in their largely settled style of living, and their deep hatred for the feroxaloid hominids living among them, such as the Ftemioq. Our scholars suppose that for some many centuries the violent and tall, mostly carnivorous feroxaloids preyed upon the smaller cobaloids and bofungoids, and it was with the arrival of vewugism that the tide was turned, and the ferroxaloids were driven under the yoke.

The state of culture in Bafozh is hardly sufficiently developed to merit particular demarcation beyond large racial/linguistic groups or sets of lifestyles. The entries found below then are particularly general for our encyclopedia, based largely on anthropological notes by our explorers and colonial administrators.

many Asyum in the inner jungles are not J’ur at all. The Asyum people have a wide range of lifestyles, from the hardly contracted jungle peoples, to the nomads plainsmen, to the settled cultures who fish the phosphorescent jellies that seem to abound in the Zhadnozhogid sea. Those Asyum princes in Nywut have also began to import Nuddi root, for the purposes of growing and exporting it.

The charchlands refers to all those lands including Charch, Cherass, and Gokam. The Gokam appear to not be linguistically related at all to the Charch or Cherassians, but nonetheless are usually classed as being charchlanders. The charchlands are one of the most settled parts of bafozh, and the thatched houses of charchland are a typical quaint depiction in artwork. They are fractious people, and are quick to arms, and are very angry. A typical curse in their land is: ‘six birds are not enough.’ The idiom is hardly translatable, but the author assures the reader of this encyclopedia that it is quite biting.

For material purposes, the forest dwellers of southern Bafozh may be classed into one sort of people, despite speaking a variety of languages. They hunt the great beasts of southern forests, and fish the many rivers of this land. They are little more than simple animist peoples.

The beast men of the north include the Hrussan and Hohraethy, but they are different sorts. The Hrussan are dentaloids, with large, menacing jaws, which they usually use to grind up plants, but occasionally smash into each other and their enemies. The Hohraethy are oriental gigantoids, with spectacular ‘coneheads’. It is supposed that the dry and arid landscapes attracted hominids with the capacity to survive on little and dry foods.
The Azuroids of the Central Belt

The Azuroids of the central belt of Bafozh are only of note for their strange and frightening blue skin. Dwelling in the jungles, it is sometimes supposed that such a skin was adapted to picking up certain tones of light, or blending in with lush foliage. Our biologists and naturalists are generally quite stumped, but a notable trade in their skin, as well as the habit of capturing them to bring back to our zoos, is already beginning.

Herein is found entries related to the Island peoples of the world. One might notice a number of curious features of those living in the Islands, in that they seem to display freakish differences from most hominidae. The Orgehi of the north display a degree of Gigantism, and have furry coats, whereas the Island people of the Ishnapt are all oriental insuloids, small and delicate people who seemingly have adapted to scarce food supplies. Most of these peoples display remarkably little development beyond the Tuqqikian of Shobgizob.

The Ogrehi are troglodytic peoples living in the northern reaches of Paukzhodo, as well as a few small islands in the surrounding area, hence why this region in many languages is 'troglodytica' or 'land-of-cavedwellers'. They seem to be a unique class of hominids that have adapted especially to the frigid lands they live in, growing large and hairy coats. They are generally in a state of depraved barbarism, eating each other's flesh in war-raids, living in caves, and mainly subsisting off of the hunting of large boreal creatures or fatty pinnipeds caught on the coast, as well as berries and nuts in the summers. However, off the coast of Paukzhodo, on the small island of Badath, they have been organised into a somewhat regular settled society. It is not clear how the Ogrehi arrived in Badath, nor why the Njutto did not occupy this region. In any case, the small kingdom of Badath was incorporated into the Rannu empire long ago, and the Ogrehi there have learned to write in Rannutan letters.

The Tuqqikian folk are a collection of oriental insuloids living mostly in Shobgizob. They are united by speaking a common collection of dialects, but are generally divided into ‘settled’ Tuqqikian and ‘bush’ Tuqqikian. The settled folk are bloodletters mostly (some have converted to Vewugism), and worshipers of a demanding high god who asks for many sacrifices, while they bush folk seem to exhibit a number of animist and shamanist folkways. They are known for their feathered dress, which they collect from the large flightless birds that live in Shobgizob and which they both hunt and (only the settled folk) keep as livestock. They are also excellent swimmers, and are known to dive deep into water to collect kelps, small molluscs and bivalves, as well as reef-fish, much like the nearby Zagkhan. In settled Tuqqikian society, the order of priests holds great sway. They value piety and fortitude, as well as humour. They describe life as a ‘cruel dream’ of the gods (or god, for the monotheists).

‘Zagkhan’ is more of a misnomer really. The many peoples who speak a Zagkhanian language are spread out across the vast Ishnapt sea, its many volcanic islands, atolls, and some of its larger islands and island chains. They are all, it seems, oriental insuloids. They are expert rafters, and build loosely knit vessels from wood and fibers, and seem to drift across the great seas using robust and fibrous sails. They are also excellent divers and fishermen like the Tuqqikian. They are socially arranged into those who are of marriageable age, and those who are not, or are married. These groups of society are strictly segregated, and young couples are expected to live apart from their larger settlements until they marry, and then they can return. This encourages a high rate of marriage. They are, as expected, largely pescetarian-frugivorous.

The Kingdom of Gaubja is a developed monarchical south Gashdzii state in the east of the continent. The ‘Gaub’ people (-ja) began their history as marches of the empire, and the Margravate of Gaub (of which the earliest record is an imperial grant of such a title in 664, still held in the imperial library in Pashdzii) slowly gave its name to both the people of the region and the later state. It’s known for its beautiful coasts and uplands in the far east, as well as for its hardy and daring seamen who fish the eastern oceans. The Gaubjan state was wracked in the mid 1270s by a particularly bloody palace coup against the old dynasty. The Pozâfauk Dynasty, which dates as early as the 800s, was overthrown and house Bodimhazh came to the throne, making the beheading of old Mozzanak II Pozâfauk their very flag. The state has experienced a number of popular jacqueries nominally in support of the Pozâfauk family, and tensions remain across Gaubjan society related to dynastic loyalty.

Gozonazh, along with Chiishozd, is one of the youngest states of Ishahfazh. As the power of the Vuyti states began to be outstripped by the increasingly wealthy and technologically advanced south Gashdzii, a number of colonial settlements were made in the fertile and temperate coastland of the far south in the mid 900s. By the early 1000s, these had organised themselves into a small federation under the protection of Gozoshovi Paptazh (968-1021), a powerful regional landowner. Paptazh gradually fashioned the federation into a private monarchy, slowly increasing his dominion over the region. Gozo’s land, as the regions of Vonjar and Yuwja came to slowly be called, formally became a monarchy in 1128, after the war of Dhaug (1121-6) with Jishanâgi settlers advancing south, when Nobamedes Paptazh (1098-1167) declared a dictatorship to organise the war effort, which he never relinquished. The court is held in Pifshop, on the river Vonjar. Gozonazh holds no deep ties to the old empire.

The ‘seven cities of the burning coast’ are usually called the Chiishozd, or the young-grass lands.
